body:
## Definition

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$, an independent orientation $o$, and, where specified, a smooth observer congruence $n$ on an open set.

[F1] The geometric data consist of a smooth boundaryless four-manifold, a smooth nondegenerate metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and a smooth timelike field $N$ selecting future direction. The time orientation does not supply a manifold orientation. ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]])

[F2] A pointwise observer is future unit timelike; its rest space is $n^\perp$. The orthogonal projection $h_n(v)=v+g(n,v)n$ has image $n^\perp$, and this three-dimensional subspace has positive-definite restricted metric. ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]], [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]])

[F3] A smooth observer congruence is a smooth future unit timelike field; its maximal integral curves and adapted charts have the domains and spatial-coordinate condition stated in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. A tetrad field and coordinate frame have the distinct meanings stated in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]].

[F4] The metric-selected connection is torsion-free and metric-compatible, with $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\frac12g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc})$. The curvature convention is $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$, $R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$, and ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]], [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]])

$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb}+\sum_e(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}).$$

The Ricci and scalar contractions are $\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and $S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$.

[F5] For each $m\ge 0$, repeated differentiation of $x^{1/2}$ gives $D^m(x^{1/2})=\bigl(\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(\frac12-j)\bigr)x^{1/2-m}$ on $(0,\infty)$; each derivative is continuous there, so $x\mapsto\sqrt{x}$ is smooth. For $m=0$ the product is empty and equals $1$; differentiating the formula at order $m$ by [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] multiplies its coefficient by $\frac12-m$, proving the next order by finite induction. The same induction with $\frac12$ replaced by any fixed real exponent $\alpha$ makes $x^\alpha$ smooth on $(0,\infty)$; in particular $\alpha=-\frac12$ covers reciprocal square-root normalizers. For each finite $k$, [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]] gives closure of $C^k$ maps under finite componentwise sums, products and composition on open Euclidean domains. Applying this for every finite $k$ shows that composing the square root with a smooth positive function preserves smoothness, as used to normalize a smooth timelike field.

[A1] The smooth tangent-bundle structure used by the existing Lorentzian and observer definitions is recorded under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Its exact statement is that each countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. No full Axiom of Choice is used by the finite local construction below. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

1.1 The normalization $n:=N/\sqrt{-g(N,N)}$ is smooth because $-g(N,N)$ is a smooth positive function and [F5] makes its positive square root smooth. Bilinearity gives $g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,N)=-\sqrt{-g(N,N)}<0$, so [F2] makes $n$ an observer at every point and hence a smooth observer congruence. This supplies an observer field without identifying it with a chart or tetrad. [F1, F2, F5, algebra]

1.2 Fix $p\in U$ and a connected chart around $p$. The four coordinate vectors form a basis at $p$. By [F2], the linear map $h_{n_p}$ has image the three-dimensional space $n_p^\perp$, so three projected coordinate vectors form a basis of $n_p^\perp$. Extend the chosen coordinate fields over the chart and project them by $h_n$; after shrinking the chart, their projections remain independent by continuity. They lie in the positive-definite rest spaces by [F2]. Apply the three finite Gram-Schmidt operations in these rest spaces; every denominator is the positive square root of a positive smooth squared norm, so [F5] makes the resulting fields smooth. Together with $E_0=n$, the three fields form a local tetrad. If needed, reverse one spatial member so the tetrad has the supplied orientation from [F1]; the sign remains fixed on the connected chart. This is a local tetrad field as in [F3], not a coordinate frame or an assertion of an adapted coordinate chart. Thus an $n$-adapted tetrad exists locally, with no global tetrad or hypersurface-orthogonality conclusion. [F1, F2, F3, F5, A1, construct, algebra]

2.1 In a length-coordinate chart, each first coordinate derivative of $g_{ab}$ has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, so the Christoffel formula in [F4] has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Each term in the curvature formula in [F4] has dimension $\mathrm m^{-2}$; contraction with dimensionless $g^{ab}$ preserves that dimension for Ricci and scalar curvature. This is coordinate-unit bookkeeping, not a physical field equation. [F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth oriented Lorentzian structure, its metric volume form, and smooth differential forms of degrees $0$ through $4$.

[F1] The oriented Lorentzian manifold has signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and each point has a neighborhood with a positively oriented smooth orthonormal tetrad. The metric volume form has value $+1$ on a positively oriented orthonormal tetrad. ([[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]], [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]], [[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]])

[F2] A smooth $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$ and has a unique local expansion in increasing coordinate wedges. ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]], [[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]])

[F3] The wedge product is the pointwise alternating product of covectors and differential forms form an associative graded-commutative algebra. ([[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]], [[prop-differential-forms-form-a-graded-commutative-algebra]])

[F4] The exterior derivative is defined by its invariant vector-field formula; it is a smooth form, and in coordinates it is $(d\alpha)_{a_0\cdots a_k}=(k+1)\partial_{[a_0}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k]}$. ([[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], [[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]], [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]])

[F5] Smooth mixed partial derivatives commute, and the exterior derivative is an $\mathbb R$-linear degree-one graded derivation of the wedge algebra. ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]])

[F6] The inverse metric raises covector slots. In an orthonormal coframe, the determinant pairing of decomposable wedges is diagonal, with diagonal entry the product of their metric signs; its component expression is the normalized contraction displayed in the Statement, since each increasing index set occurs $k!$ times in the full antisymmetric sum. ([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]])

[A1] The background tangent-bundle smooth structure inherits $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as recorded in [[def-countable-choice]]. The finite coframe calculations below use no full Axiom of Choice.

## Proof

1.1 The determinant is alternating multilinear in each list, so it defines a bilinear pairing on exterior powers. In a positively oriented orthonormal coframe, it makes the basis wedges $e^I$ orthogonal with squared norm $\epsilon_I$; in the full component contraction this same diagonal value occurs $k!$ times, canceled by the factor $1/k!$. Define $\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$ and extend linearly. If $J\ne I$ has the same size as $I$, then $e^J\wedge e^{I^c}=0$ because an index repeats. If $J=I$, then $e^I\wedge e^{I^c}=s(I,I^c)\mathrm{vol}_g$, so $e^I\wedge\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I\mathrm{vol}_g$. Bilinearity proves the characterizing identity for all forms in the coframe. The complement wedges pair each basis vector with exactly one basis vector, so this wedge pairing is nondegenerate and the characterization determines $\star_g$ uniquely. [F1, F2, F3, F6, A1, algebra, construct]

2.1 The characterizing identity uses only $g$, the orientation, and $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Any other positively oriented orthonormal coframe therefore defines the same map by uniqueness. In each smooth tetrad neighborhood the displayed matrix of $\star_g$ is constant in the smooth coframe, so its coordinate coefficients are smooth; the locally defined maps agree on overlaps and give a global smooth bundle map on the inherited smooth background [A1]. [step 1.1, F1, F2, A1, algebra]

2.2 Applying the basis formula twice gives $\star_g^2e^I=\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)e^I$. The product $\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}$ equals $-1$ because exactly one of the four $\epsilon_i$ is negative. Reversing the two blocks of sizes $k$ and $4-k$ takes $k(4-k)$ transpositions, so $s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)=(-1)^{k(4-k)}$. Their product is $(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}$, proving the square formula for each basis element and hence for every $k$-form. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For a two-form $F=\frac12F_{cd}e^c\wedge e^d$, the basis formula sends each $e^c\wedge e^d$ to its oriented complementary wedge with the product of its metric signs. In components this is $({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}$: the factor $1/2$ counts each antisymmetric pair once, and raising both indices includes the negative sign in the timelike slot. [step 1.1, F1, F6, algebra]

3.1 In a chart, [F4] gives $(d\alpha)_{a_0\cdots a_k}=(k+1)\partial_{[a_0}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k]}$. Applying it twice expresses each coefficient of $d^2\alpha$ as an alternating sum of second partial derivatives; terms paired by exchanging the first two derivative indices cancel because those mixed partials agree by [F5]. Thus $d^2\alpha=0$ in every chart and hence globally. The graded product rule is exactly the established identity in [F5]. [F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The positive-definite Hodge formula would omit the extra signature sign. It is not a supplier for this item: the single negative direction contributes $\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}=-1$ in step 2.1. No metric field equation, Maxwell postulate, global potential, or physical interpretation is used.

## Statement

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with the curvature convention and tensors of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Let $\Omega:M\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth and dimensionless, and put $\widetilde g=\Omega^2g$ with the same orientation. Use the metric-selected connection and its tensor derivative of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Define the smooth one-form and its contractions by

$$u:=\Omega^{-1}d\Omega,\qquad H_{ab}:=(\nabla_a u)_b,\qquad \theta:=g^{ab}H_{ab},\qquad s:=g^{ab}u_au_b.$$

Then $H_{ab}=H_{ba}$ and

$$\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-2H_{ab}-g_{ab}\theta+2u_au_b-2g_{ab}s,$$

$$\widetilde S=\Omega^{-2}(S-6\theta-6s),$$

$$\widetilde G_{ab}=G_{ab}-2H_{ab}+2u_au_b+2g_{ab}\theta+g_{ab}s.$$

All curvature conventions are those stated in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. These are mathematical transformation identities, not an assertion that the Einstein equation is conformally invariant.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, smooth positive $\Omega$, and the metric-selected connections of $g$ and $\widetilde g$. The inherited geometric setup carries $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in [A1].

[F1] The geometry is smooth, oriented and time-oriented, with nondegenerate Lorentz metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; its smooth real forms and metric volume form have the definitions of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]].

[F2] Curvature is $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$, with $R^a{}_{bcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=g^{ac}R_{abcd}$, $S=g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, and $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 Sg_{ab}$. ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]])

[F3] For either smooth Lorentz metric $h=g$ or $h=\widetilde g$, the metric-selected connection is affine and torsion-free and has Christoffel formula $\Gamma[h]^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12h^{ad}(\partial_bh_{dc}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc})$. ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]], [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]])

[F4] For a type $(1,2)$ tensor $C$, the tensor derivative has components $(\nabla_{\partial_c}C)^a{}_{db}=\partial_cC^a{}_{db}+\Gamma^a{}_{ec}C^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^e{}_{dc}C^a{}_{eb}-\Gamma^e{}_{bc}C^a{}_{de}$; it commutes with contractions and annihilates $g$ and $g^{-1}$. ([[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]])

[F5] The exterior derivative sends a smooth $k$-form to a smooth $(k+1)$-form, has coordinate formula $(d\beta)_{a_0\ldots a_k}=(k+1)\partial_{[a_0}\beta_{a_1\ldots a_k]}$, and obeys $d^2=0$ and the graded product rule. ([[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]])

[F6] For $x>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}$; the chain rule holds for total derivatives. ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F7] For each finite $k$, finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps and compositions of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$. Applying this at every finite $k$ in smooth manifold charts shows that finite sums, products and compositions of smooth maps are smooth. ([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]])

[F8] For either metric-selected connection, with the curvature convention of [F2], the coordinate curvature formula is $R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb}+\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}$, with summation over $e$. ([[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]])

[A1] The inherited choice assumption is Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, not full Choice. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

1.1 In a chart, $\partial_a\widetilde g_{bc}=\Omega^2(\partial_ag_{bc}+2u_ag_{bc})$ and $\widetilde g^{ad}=\Omega^{-2}g^{ad}$. Substituting these into [F3] cancels the common $\Omega^2$ and gives $\widetilde\Gamma^a{}_{bc}-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=C^a{}_{bc}:=\delta^a_bu_c+\delta^a_cu_b-g_{bc}u^a$, where $u^a=g^{ab}u_b$. Iterating the derivative formula in [F6] gives $D^m(r^{-1})=(-1)^m m!r^{-m-1}$ for every integer $m\ge0$ and $r>0$; all these derivatives are continuous, so $r\mapsto r^{-1}$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$. Its composition with $\Omega$ is smooth by [F7], and $d\Omega$ is a smooth one-form by [F5], so $u$ and the displayed components $C^a{}_{bc}$ are smooth. Finally, define $A(X,Y):=\widetilde\nabla_XY-\nabla_XY$ for smooth local vector fields. The affine-connection rules in [F3] give $A(fX,Y)=fA(X,Y)$ and $A(X,fY)=fA(X,Y)$ for every smooth function $f$, while its components are the smooth differences $C^a{}_{bc}$; hence $A$ is a smooth tensor of type $(1,2)$ with those components. [given, F1, F3, F5, F6, F7, A1, algebra]

2.1 By [F5], $0=d(1)=d(\Omega^{-1}\Omega)=\Omega^{-1}d\Omega+\Omega\,d(\Omega^{-1})$, so $d(\Omega^{-1})=-\Omega^{-2}d\Omega$. Therefore $du=d(\Omega^{-1})\wedge d\Omega+\Omega^{-1}d^2\Omega=-\Omega^{-2}d\Omega\wedge d\Omega=0$. Torsion freedom in [F3] gives $(du)_{ab}=\nabla_a u_b-\nabla_bu_a$, hence $H_{ab}=H_{ba}$. [F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Apply the coordinate curvature formula [F8] to $g$ and $\widetilde g$ and subtract, using $\widetilde\Gamma=\Gamma+C$ from step 1.1. Since $C$ is a tensor, [F4] gives $(\nabla_cC)^a{}_{db}-(\nabla_dC)^a{}_{cb}=\partial_cC^a{}_{db}-\partial_dC^a{}_{cb}+\Gamma^a{}_{ce}C^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}C^e{}_{cb}+\Gamma^e{}_{db}C^a{}_{ce}-\Gamma^e{}_{cb}C^a{}_{de}$; the two covariant-derivative terms acting on the lower curvature-direction slots $d,c$ cancel because $\Gamma^e{}_{cd}=\Gamma^e{}_{dc}$, while the lower $b$-slot contributions are the last two displayed terms. These are exactly the partial-derivative and mixed $\Gamma C$ terms in the subtraction, and the remaining terms are $C^a{}_{ce}C^e{}_{db}-C^a{}_{de}C^e{}_{cb}$. Therefore $\widetilde R^a{}_{bcd}-R^a{}_{bcd}=\nabla_cC^a{}_{db}-\nabla_dC^a{}_{cb}+C^a{}_{ce}C^e{}_{db}-C^a{}_{de}C^e{}_{cb}$. [F2, F4, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Contracting $a$ with $c$ as in [F2], the derivative terms are $\nabla_aC^a{}_{db}-\nabla_dC^a{}_{ab}$. The definition of $C$ gives $C^a{}_{ab}=4u_b$ and, using $\nabla g=0$ from [F4], $\nabla_aC^a{}_{db}=H_{db}+H_{bd}-g_{db}\theta=2H_{bd}-g_{db}\theta$ by step 2.1. Thus their difference is $-2H_{bd}-g_{bd}\theta$. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The first quadratic contraction is $C^a{}_{ae}C^e{}_{db}=4u_e(\delta^e_du_b+\delta^e_bu_d-g_{db}u^e)=8u_bu_d-4g_{bd}s$. Expanding the second contraction into its nine terms gives $C^a{}_{de}C^e{}_{ab}=u_du_b+u_du_b-g_{db}s+4u_du_b+u_du_b-u_du_b-u_du_b-g_{db}s+u_du_b=6u_bu_d-2g_{bd}s$. Their difference is $2u_bu_d-2g_{bd}s$. Combining this with step 3.1 proves the Ricci transformation in the Statement. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Contracting the Ricci transformation with $\widetilde g^{ab}=\Omega^{-2}g^{ab}$ gives $\widetilde S=\Omega^{-2}(S-2\theta-4\theta+2s-8s)=\Omega^{-2}(S-6\theta-6s)$. [F2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 By definition, $\widetilde G_{ab}=\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ab}-\tfrac12\widetilde S\,\widetilde g_{ab}$. Substituting the Ricci formula from step 4.1 and $\widetilde S\,\widetilde g_{ab}=(S-6\theta-6s)g_{ab}$ from step 5.1 cancels the scalar-curvature terms and leaves $G_{ab}-2H_{ab}+2u_au_b+2g_{ab}\theta+g_{ab}s$. This is the claimed Einstein-tensor formula. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The curvature sign and Ricci contraction were taken from the inspected Lorentzian supplier [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. The conformal identities above were derived with that convention; no Riemannian curvature formula or sign convention is imported.

## Statement

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be as in [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], let $\Omega:M\to(0,\infty)$ be a smooth dimensionless function, and set $\widetilde g=\Omega^2g$ with the same orientation $o$. For every smooth $k$-form $\beta$, $0\le k\le4$,

$$\star_{\widetilde g}\beta=\Omega^{4-2k}\star_g\beta.$$

In degree $2$ the Hodge star is unchanged. This is a statement about the Hodge operators of two conformally related Lorentz metrics; it asserts no conformal invariance of any curvature or field equation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, a smooth positive function $\Omega$, and a smooth $k$-form $\beta$.

[F1] The Hodge star is uniquely characterized by $\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\mathrm{vol}_g$ for all $k$-forms $\alpha,\beta$. ([[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]])

[A1] The smooth tangent-bundle background inherits $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from [[def-countable-choice]]; the pointwise scaling calculation below is finite-dimensional and uses no full Choice.

## Proof

1.1 On the inherited smooth manifold background [A1], since $\widetilde g=\Omega^2g$ and $\Omega>0$, its inverse is $\widetilde g^{-1}=\Omega^{-2}g^{-1}$. The exterior pairing of two $k$-forms contains exactly $k$ inverse-metric factors, so $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{\widetilde g}=\Omega^{-2k}\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g$. In a positively oriented chart, $\det(\widetilde g_{ab})=\Omega^8\det(g_{ab})$; therefore the metric volume form scales as $\mathrm{vol}_{\widetilde g}=\Omega^4\mathrm{vol}_g$. [given, F1, A1, algebra]

2.1 Applying the defining identity in [F1] with $\widetilde g$ in place of $g$ and substituting step 1.1 gives, for every $k$-form $\alpha$, $\alpha\wedge\star_{\widetilde g}\beta=\Omega^{-2k}\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\Omega^4\mathrm{vol}_g=\alpha\wedge\bigl(\Omega^{4-2k}\star_g\beta\bigr)$. ## Statement

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ and a smooth real two-form $F$ be as in [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. $$\operatorname{vol}_{\widetilde g}=\Omega^4\operatorname{vol}_g,\qquad \iota_{\widetilde j}\operatorname{vol}_{\widetilde g}=\iota_j\operatorname{vol}_g,\qquad \widetilde T_{ab}=\Omega^{-2}T_{ab},\qquad \widetilde T^{ab}=\Omega^{-6}T^{ab}.$$

If $n$ is a $g$-unit timelike vector, then $\widetilde n:=\Omega^{-1}n$ is $\widetilde g$-unit timelike and $\widetilde T(\widetilde n,\widetilde n)=\Omega^{-4}T(n,n)$. On any oriented integration domain where the integral exists, or for a compactly supported action difference, the quadratic integral $\int F_{ab}F^{ab}\operatorname{vol}_g$ is unchanged. ## Definition

Use the smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, metric signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and arbitrary smooth real two-form $F$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Define the derived parameters

$$\varepsilon_0:=\frac{1}{\mu_0c^2},\qquad \kappa:=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4},\qquad \alpha:=\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{2\mu_0}},\qquad \mathcal F:=\alpha F.$$

Thus $\varepsilon_0$ has unit $\mathrm{C^2\,s^2\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$, $\kappa$ has unit $\mathrm{m\,J^{-1}}$, $\alpha$ has unit $\mathrm{C\,s\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$, and the components $\mathcal F_{ab}$ have unit $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. For a physical mass $M_{\!p}>0$ in kilograms, signed charge $Q_e$ in coulombs, and angular momentum $J_{\mathrm{ang}}$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$, define the geometric length parameters

$$m_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\frac{GM_{\!p}}{c^2},\qquad q_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\sqrt{\frac{G}{4\pi\varepsilon_0c^4}}\,Q_e,\qquad a_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\frac{J_{\mathrm{ang}}}{M_{\!p}c}.$$

For a supplied magnetic-flux parameter $\Phi_B$ in webers, also define $p_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\alpha\Phi_B/(4\pi)$ in metres. This is only a conversion of an already specified flux value; it asserts neither a global potential nor a magnetic source. The inverse parameter maps are $M_{\!p}=c^2m_{\mathrm{geo}}/G$, $Q_e=\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_0c^4/G}\,q_{\mathrm{geo}}$, $J_{\mathrm{ang}}=M_{\!p}c\,a_{\mathrm{geo}}$, and $\Phi_B=4\pi p_{\mathrm{geo}}/\alpha$.

## Statement

$$\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F):=F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd},$$

where indices are raised with $g^{-1}$. Then the following equations for the same metric and two-form are equivalent:

$$G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F),$$

$$G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=2\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F),$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g)-\Lambda g_{ab}=2\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F).$$

These are algebraic equivalences between tensor equations. No Maxwell equation, matter model, limiting procedure or physical solution is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth Lorentzian geometry and positive parameters of [[def-emg-geometric-scaling]], a smooth real two-form $F$, and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. [A1] The only inherited choice assumption is Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, stated as choosing one element from each set in a countable family of nonempty sets. ([[def-countable-choice]])

1.1 Contracting the displayed definition of $\mathcal Q$ gives $g^{ab}\mathcal Q_{ab}=F_{ac}F^{ac}-\tfrac14(g^{ab}g_{ab})F_{cd}F^{cd}=F_{cd}F^{cd}-F_{cd}F^{cd}=0$, because the metric dimension is four. Thus $\mathcal Q$ is trace-free. [given, F2, A1, algebra]

1.2 Each term of $\mathcal Q(g,F)$ contains exactly two factors linear in $F$, so for every scalar $s$, $\mathcal Q(g,sF)=s^2\mathcal Q(g,F)$. In particular, $\mathcal Q(g,\mathcal F)=\alpha^2\mathcal Q(g,F)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Since $2\alpha^2=\kappa/\mu_0$ by [F1], the right-hand side $(\kappa/\mu_0)\mathcal Q(g,F)$ equals $2\mathcal Q(g,\mathcal F)$; replacing it in the first equation proves equivalence of the first two equations in both directions. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 By [F2], tracing the second equation gives $-S+4\Lambda=0$, since $g^{ab}G_{ab}=S-\tfrac12(4)S=-S$ and the right-hand side is trace-free by step 1.1. Hence $S=4\Lambda$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substituting $S=4\Lambda$ into $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}$ gives $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-2\Lambda g_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\Lambda g_{ab}$, proving the second equation implies the third. Conversely, tracing the third equation and using step 1.1 gives $S-4\Lambda=0$; substituting this into $G_{ab}$ recovers the second equation. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Define $\mathbb C\llbracket g\rrbracket$ to be the set of coefficient sequences $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$, written $\sum_{n\ge0}a_ng^n$, with coefficientwise equality and addition and Cauchy multiplication: the coefficient of $g^n$ in a product is $\sum_{k=0}^na_kb_{n-k}$, a finite sum. Formal membership makes no numerical convergence assertion. For numerical evaluation use $g^0:=1$ for every $g$, including $g=0$; numerical convergence means convergence of the partial sums in $\mathbb C$. In the extended nonnegative reals $[0,+\infty]$, the numerical radius of a coefficient sequence is

$$R:=\sup\{r\in[0,+\infty): \sum_{n\ge0}a_ng^n\text{ converges for every }g\in\mathbb C\text{ with }|g|<r\},$$

where the supremum is taken in the extended order, so $R=+\infty$ when the set is unbounded. The claim to refute is that every element of $\mathbb C\llbracket g\rrbracket$ has $R>0$.

For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, define $n!:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}k$, with the empty product $0!:=1$; thus $(n+1)!=(n+1)n!$. View these integer products as coefficients in $\mathbb C$ through the canonical embedding $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

1.1 Each $n!$ is a finite complex number by [F1], so the sequence $(n!)_{n\ge0}$ defines an element $S(g)=\sum_{n\ge0}n!g^n$ of $\mathbb C\llbracket g\rrbracket$ by [A1], irrespective of numerical convergence. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 Fix any $g\ne0$ and put $t_n=n!g^n$. 2.1 If the numerical series $\sum_nt_n$ converged, its partial sums $s_N:=\sum_{n=0}^Nt_n$ would converge, so $t_n=s_n-s_{n-1}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$; step 1.2 rules this out for every nonzero $g$. ## Remarks

This example separates coefficientwise formal algebra from numerical convergence. It proves no convergence, summability, or divergence claim for any particular QFT perturbation series. A truncation error requires a separate estimate for a specified analytic model; formal coefficient identities alone do not provide one.

## Definition

A **unital complex star algebra** is a complex vector space $A$ with a complex-bilinear associative product $(a,b)\mapsto ab$, a specified unit $1_A$, and a conjugate-linear map $a\mapsto a^*$ such that, for all $a,b\in A$,

$$ (ab)^*=b^*a^*,\qquad (a^*)^*=a,\qquad 1_A^*=1_A. $$

A **positive normalized state** on $A$ is a complex-linear functional $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$ such that $\omega(1_A)=1$ and $\omega(a^*a)$ is a real nonnegative number for every $a\in A$. This is an algebraic definition: no norm, topology, boundedness condition, or completion is part of the data.

## Form conventions

A sesquilinear form $B:A\times A\to\mathbb C$ is taken to be linear in its first variable and conjugate-linear in its second. It is **Hermitian** when $B(a,b)=\overline{B(b,a)}$ for all $a,b\in A$, **positive semidefinite** when $B(a,a)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $a\in A$, and has **radical**

$$\operatorname{rad}B:=\{a\in A:B(a,b)=0\text{ for every }b\in A\}.$$

For a Hermitian form this left radical also equals $\{a\in A:B(b,a)=0\text{ for every }b\in A\}$.

## Statement

Let $A$ be a unital complex star algebra and let $\omega$ be a positive normalized state on $A$ ([[def-qft-involutive-algebra-state]]). Define $q(a):=\omega(a^*a)$ and $N_\omega:=\{a\in A:q(a)=0\}$. Then

$$|\omega(b^*a)|^2\le q(a)q(b)\qquad(a,b\in A).$$

The form $(a,b)_\omega:=\omega(b^*a)$ is Hermitian and positive semidefinite, $N_\omega$ is its radical and a complex linear subspace, and $N_\omega$ is a left ideal: $c a\in N_\omega$ whenever $a\in N_\omega$ and $c\in A$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A unital complex star algebra $A$ and a positive normalized state $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$.

[F1] [[def-qft-involutive-algebra-state]]: multiplication is complex-bilinear and associative, $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$, and $\omega$ is complex-linear with $\omega(1_A)=1$ and real nonnegative $\omega(a^*a)$ for every $a\in A$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $X:=\omega(a^*b)$ and $Y:=\omega(b^*a)$. Positivity makes both $q(a+b)=q(a)+X+Y+q(b)$ and $q(a+ib)=q(a)+iX-iY+q(b)$ real; their imaginary parts give $\operatorname{Im}(X+Y)=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(X-Y)=0$, hence $Y=\overline X$. Thus $(a,b)_\omega=\omega(b^*a)$ is Hermitian. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $q(b)>0$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$, positivity and the star-algebra laws give $0\le q(a+zb)=q(a)+zX+\overline z\,\overline X+|z|^2q(b)$. Taking $z=-\overline X/q(b)$ yields $0\le q(a)-|X|^2/q(b)$, so $|\omega(b^*a)|^2=|Y|^2=|X|^2\le q(a)q(b)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $q(b)=0$. If $X\ne0$, taking $z=-t\overline X$ for real $t>q(a)/(2|X|^2)$ makes $q(a+zb)=q(a)-2t|X|^2<0$, contradicting positivity. Hence $X=Y=0$, so the same Cauchy–Schwarz inequality holds when $q(b)=0$; if instead $q(a)=0$ and $q(b)>0$, step 2.1 forces $Y=0$ as well. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $a\in N_\omega$, steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $(a,b)_\omega=0$ for every $b\in A$; conversely $(a,a)_\omega=0$ means $a\in N_\omega$. Thus $N_\omega$ is exactly the radical and is a linear subspace. For $c\in A$, set $d:=c^*ca$. Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to $a,d$ gives $|\omega(d^*a)|^2\le q(a)q(d)=0$, while $d^*a=a^*c^*ca=(ca)^*(ca)$; therefore $ca\in N_\omega$. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Operator conventions

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first variable. An operator on $H$ is a linear map $T:D(T)\to H$ whose domain $D(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H$; it is densely defined when $D(T)$ is dense in $H$. It is bounded when some $C\geq0$ satisfies $\|Tx\|\leq C\|x\|$ for all $x\in D(T)$, and unbounded when no such $C$ exists. No boundedness of the operators $\pi_\omega(a)$ is assumed here.

For a complex vector space $E$, $\operatorname{End}(E)$ denotes the set of complex-linear maps from $E$ to itself. The product norm on $H\times H$ is $\|(x,y)\|_\times:=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2}$.

For a densely defined $T$, define its Hilbert-space adjoint by

$$D(T^*):=\{y\in H:\text{there is }z\in H\text{ such that }(Tx,y)=(x,z)\text{ for every }x\in D(T)\},\qquad T^*y:=z.$$

The vector $z$ is unique because $D(T)$ is dense. The graph of $T$ is $G(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\times H$. The operator $T$ is **symmetric** when $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and $T^*x=Tx$ for every $x\in D(T)$; it is **self-adjoint** when $D(T)=D(T^*)$ and the same equality holds there. It is **closable** when the closure of $G(T)$ in the product norm on $H\times H$ is the graph of an operator, denoted $\overline T$. A symmetric operator is **essentially self-adjoint** when it is closable and $\overline T$ is self-adjoint.

## Statement

Let $A$ be a complex vector space with a complex-bilinear associative product, unit $1_A$, and conjugate-linear involution satisfying $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$, $(a^*)^*=a$ and $1_A^*=1_A$. $$([a],[b])_\omega:=\omega(b^*a),$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A unital complex star algebra $A$, a positive normalized state $\omega$, and Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as stated above.

[F1] [[lem-qft-positive-state-cauchy-schwarz]]: $(a,b)_\omega=\omega(b^*a)$ is a Hermitian positive semidefinite form, its radical is $N_\omega=\{a\in A:(a,b)_\omega=0\text{ for every }b\in A\}$, and $N_\omega$ is a left ideal; also $|\omega(b^*a)|^2\le\omega(a^*a)\omega(b^*b)$, including zero-norm cases.

[F2] [[thm-completion-of-an-inner-product-space-is-hilbert]]: assuming Countable Choice, the norm completion of a real or complex inner-product space has a unique extended inner product inducing the completion norm and is a Hilbert space. Its proof uses Countable Choice to select countably many approximants; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed here.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], $N_\omega$ is a subspace and every element of it pairs to zero with every element of $A$. Thus $([a],[b])_\omega=\omega(b^*a)$ is independent of both representatives; it is Hermitian and nonnegative, and $([a],[a])_\omega=0$ holds exactly when $a\in N_\omega$, so the quotient pairing is positive definite. [F1, given]

1.2 For $a,b\in A$, replacing $b$ by $b+n$ with $n\in N_\omega$ changes $ab$ by $an\in N_\omega$ because $N_\omega$ is a left ideal by [F1]; hence $\pi_\omega(a)[b]=[ab]$ is well defined. Bilinearity, associativity and $1_A$ give $\pi_\omega(a+b)=\pi_\omega(a)+\pi_\omega(b)$, $\pi_\omega(\lambda a)=\lambda\pi_\omega(a)$, $\pi_\omega(ab)=\pi_\omega(a)\pi_\omega(b)$ and $\pi_\omega(1_A)=I_{\mathcal D_\omega}$, and left multiplication keeps $\mathcal D_\omega$ invariant. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the quotient inner-product space $\mathcal D_\omega$; under the stated Countable Choice assumption this gives the Hilbert completion $H_\omega$ and a dense isometric embedding of $\mathcal D_\omega$, which we identify with its image. This is the only completion invoked. [F2, given, step 1.1]

2.2 For $a,b,c\in A$, the quotient form gives $(\pi_\omega(a)[b],[c])_\omega=\omega(c^*ab)=([b],\pi_\omega(a^*)[c])_\omega$. By the definition of the Hilbert-space adjoint, this identity for all $[b]\in\mathcal D_\omega$ shows $[c]\in D(\pi_\omega(a)^*)$ and $\pi_\omega(a)^*[c]=\pi_\omega(a^*)[c]$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 Since $([1_A],[1_A])_\omega=\omega(1_A)=1$, $\Omega_\omega$ is a unit vector. Also $\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega=[a]$ for every $a\in A$, so its algebraic orbit is exactly $\mathcal D_\omega$ and is dense. Finally $(\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega)_\omega=([a],[1_A])_\omega=\omega(a)$, recovering the state. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.4 Let $(H',\mathcal D',\rho,\Omega')$ be another algebraically cyclic *-representation of $A$ with common invariant dense domain $\mathcal D'=\rho(A)\Omega'$, $\rho(a^*)=\rho(a)^*|_{\mathcal D'}$, and $\omega(a)=(\rho(a)\Omega',\Omega')$. Define $U[a]:=\rho(a)\Omega'$. If $[a]=[0]$, then $\|\rho(a)\Omega'\|^2=\omega(a^*a)=0$, so $U$ is well defined; and for $a,b\in A$, $(U[a],U[b])=\omega(b^*a)=([a],[b])_\omega$ by the representation's adjoint identity. Thus $U$ is an isometry from $\mathcal D_\omega$ onto the dense subspace $\mathcal D'$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Suppose $x_n\in\mathcal D_\omega$, $x_n\to0$ in $H_\omega$, and $\pi_\omega(a)x_n\to y$ in $H_\omega$. For each $z\in\mathcal D_\omega$, step 2.2 gives $(y,z)_\omega=\lim_n(\pi_\omega(a)x_n,z)_\omega=\lim_n(x_n,\pi_\omega(a^*)z)_\omega=0$. Density forces $y=0$. Therefore the closed graph relation of $\pi_\omega(a)$ contains no two distinct outputs over one input: their difference would be a nonzero pair $(0,y)$. The graph closure is a graph, so $\pi_\omega(a)$ is closable. In particular, if $a=a^*$ then $\pi_\omega(a)$ is symmetric on $\mathcal D_\omega$; this does not prove essential self-adjointness. [step 2.2, given]

4.1 The isometry extends uniquely from the dense domain to a unitary $\overline U:H_\omega\to H'$ because its range $\mathcal D'$ is dense. It sends $\Omega_\omega$ to $\Omega'$ and, for $[b]\in\mathcal D_\omega$, $\overline U\pi_\omega(a)[b]=\rho(ab)\Omega'=\rho(a)\overline U[b]$; hence it intertwines the representations on the common domains. Uniqueness follows because every vector of $\mathcal D_\omega$ has the form $\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega$. [step 2.3, step 2.4, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume Countable Choice, the hypothesis used to form the Hilbert completion in [[thm-qft-algebraic-gns-domain]]. The claim that positivity and the Weyl relations alone make every GNS one-parameter unitary group $t\mapsto\pi(W(tv))$ strongly continuous for every $v\ne0$ is false, even for the algebraic Weyl algebra of the standard symplectic plane.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $S=\mathbb R^2$, the displayed nondegenerate alternating form $\sigma$, and the algebraic Weyl relations above.

[F1] [[thm-qft-algebraic-gns-domain]]: under Countable Choice, a positive normalized state on a unital complex star algebra has a Hilbert-space GNS representation on a common invariant dense domain, with cyclic unit vector and state recovery.

[A1] The form $\sigma$ is real-bilinear and alternating: $\sigma(f,g)=-\sigma(g,f)$ and $\sigma(f,f)=0$ for every $f,g\in S$.

## Example data

Let $S=\mathbb R^2$ with standard symplectic form $\sigma((q,p),(q',p')):=qp'-pq'$. Define $A_W$ to be the complex vector space of finite linear combinations of formal basis elements $W(f)$, $f\in S$, with bilinear multiplication and involution specified on basis elements by

$$W(f)W(g):=e^{-i\sigma(f,g)/2}W(f+g),\qquad W(f)^*:=W(-f),\qquad 1:=W(0).$$

For the false claim, a positive normalized functional is a complex-linear $\omega:A_W\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(1)=1$ and $\omega(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a$. Define

$$\omega(W(f)):=\begin{cases}1,&f=0,\\0,&f\ne0,\end{cases}$$

and extend linearly to finite sums. This Weyl algebra is algebraic: its vectors have finite support, and no norm or topology on $A_W$ is assumed. The Hilbert-space strong continuity considered below is norm continuity of each GNS orbit $t\mapsto\pi(W(tv))\xi$.

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Bilinearity of $\sigma$ gives $\sigma(f,g)+\sigma(f+g,h)=\sigma(g,h)+\sigma(f,g+h)$, so the phase factors in $(W(f)W(g))W(h)$ and $W(f)(W(g)W(h))$ agree. Also $(W(f)W(g))^*=e^{i\sigma(f,g)/2}W(-f-g)=W(-g)W(-f)$ by alternation, and $W(0)$ is a two-sided unit. Thus the displayed operations define a unital complex star algebra. [given, A1, algebra]

1.2 For $a=\sum_{f\in F}c_fW(f)$ with finite support $F\subset S$, the Weyl relation gives $a^*a=\sum_{f,g\in F}\overline{c_f}c_g e^{i\sigma(f,g)/2}W(g-f)$. Only the terms $g=f$ contribute to $\omega(a^*a)$, and $\sigma(f,f)=0$, so $\omega(a^*a)=\sum_{f\in F}|c_f|^2\ge0$; also $\omega(W(0))=1$. Hence $\omega$ is a positive normalized state. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], its GNS quotient has dense span of the classes $[W(f)]$. For $f,g\in S$, $([W(f)],[W(g)])_\omega=\omega(W(g)^*W(f))$ is $1$ if $f=g$ and $0$ otherwise; these classes are an orthonormal family with dense span. Left multiplication satisfies $\pi(W(h))[W(f)]=e^{-i\sigma(h,f)/2}[W(h+f)]$, so it permutes this orthonormal family with unit-modulus phases and extends to a unitary on the Hilbert completion, with inverse $\pi(W(-h))$. [F1, given, step 1.2]

3.1 Fix $v\in S\setminus\{0\}$ and put $U(t):=\pi(W(tv))$ for $t\in\mathbb R$. Since $\sigma(tv,sv)=ts\sigma(v,v)=0$, the Weyl relation gives $U(t)U(s)=U(t+s)$ and $U(0)=I$. For every $t\ne0$, $U(t)\Omega=[W(tv)]$ is orthogonal to $\Omega=[W(0)]$, and both are unit vectors; thus $\|U(t)\Omega-\Omega\|=\sqrt2$. This orbit is not continuous at $0$, so $U$ is not strongly continuous. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Suppose a dense linear subspace $E$ had a norm derivative $\lim_{t\to0}(U(t)\xi-\xi)/t$ for every $\xi\in E$. Each such orbit would be continuous at $0$. For any $x\in H_\omega$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\xi\in E$ with $\|x-\xi\|<\varepsilon/3$; unitarity gives $\|U(t)x-x\|\le2\|x-\xi\|+\|U(t)\xi-\xi\|$, so continuity on $E$ would imply continuity at $0$ for every $x$, contradicting step 3.1 at $x=\Omega$. Therefore no dense domain supports a norm-differentiable generator for this unitary group. The example is purely algebraic and asserts no physical preparation or relativistic vacuum. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For a spatial wave vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, with each component in
$\mathrm m^{-1}$ and the Euclidean norm, define
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, with
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here $\omega_\mu$ is the temporal wave number, not the
SI angular frequency; the corresponding SI angular frequency is
$c\omega_\mu$. Energy and momentum are $E=\hbar c\omega_\mu$ in joules and
$\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With
$p=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$, the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

For a selected local action represented on a chart region
$\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by
$$\frac{S}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathcal U}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\,d^4x,\quad d^4x:=dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3,$$
the natural Lagrangian density $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has unit
$\mathrm m^{-4}$. Since $x^0=ct$, the corresponding SI Lagrangian density is
$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SI}}:=\hbar c\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ and has unit
$\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. This unit conversion alone does not identify a
Lagrangian density with the model's Hamiltonian energy density.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
use the formal field symbols $\phi_{\rm n}$ and $\psi_{\rm n}$ in the selected
scalar and Dirac kinetic terms, assigning them length degrees $-1$ and
$-3/2$, respectively. These are the dimensions fixed by those free kinetic
terms, not exact scaling dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous
dimensions, when present, are separate quantities. These symbols do not
assert pointwise field maps or operator fields; a model supplies its field
space and regularity. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

In a supplied four-component spinor representation, let
$\gamma^a\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C^4)$, $a=0,1,2,3$, be
dimensionless linear maps satisfying
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}:=\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a
=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$, where $I_4$ is the identity map. Set $\beta:=\gamma^0$
and $\alpha^i:=\beta\gamma^i$; then $\beta^2=I_4$ and
$\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$. For a supplied four-component spinor $\psi$ write
$\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta$. The effective Clifford metric is $-\eta$.
A supplied free Dirac model may use
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$ for its model-supplied spinor field
$\psi$; that model supplies its field domain and regularity. The phase and
Clifford choices are conventions; this item proves no representation or field
equation.

If a selected model supplies a complex Hilbert space $\mathscr H$ as in
[[def-hilbert-space]], a complex-linear Hamiltonian operator
$H:D(H)\to\mathscr H$ with model-specified linear domain $D(H)\subseteq\mathscr H$
and SI energy unit joules, and an evolution family $U(t):\mathscr H\to\mathscr H$
for $t\in I\subseteq\mathbb R$ in seconds, the convention is
$U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$. Each $U(t)$ is a surjective complex-linear map
satisfying $\langle U(t)\xi,U(t)\zeta\rangle=\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle$
for all $\xi,\zeta\in\mathscr H$; write $U(t)^*:=U(t)^{-1}$. The exponent
is dimensionless because $\hbar$ has unit $\mathrm{J\,s}$. For any
model-supplied complex-linear operator $O:D(O)\to\mathscr H$, with specified
linear domain $D(O)\subseteq\mathscr H$, define its Heisenberg conjugate by
$$O_H(t):=U(t)^*O\,U(t),\quad
D(O_H(t)):=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:U(t)\xi\in D(O)\}.$$
The model supplies these domains and the evolution; this dictionary constructs
no Hamiltonian, evolution family, or field representation. Where a free-field
module uses an inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the
repository's first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction. It
asserts only matrix-element continuity and the stated linear maps; all further
operator properties, locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior must be supplied by a constructed
model. Test-function units can be chosen so a specified smeared observable is
dimensionless; there is no universal test-function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** SI base-unit identities, the stated Minkowski coordinate convention, and the canonical four-dimensional kinetic terms used only to check engineering dimensions.

[A1] For dimensional bookkeeping use $1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $1\,\mathrm C=1\,\mathrm{A\,s}$, $1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$, and $1\,\mathrm T=1\,\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$.

[A2] The canonical engineering-dimension check uses the local-action normalization $S/\hbar=\int\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}\,d^4x$, dimensionless $S/\hbar$, four-volume of degree $+4$, and the four-dimensional free kinetic densities $\partial\phi\,\partial\phi$, $\bar\psi i\gamma^a\partial_a\psi$, and $f_{ab}f^{ab}$ with $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_b a_a$. It assigns $\bar\psi$ the same engineering degree as $\psi$. This is a normalization convention, not an existence or scaling theorem.

[L1] [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]: every inertial-chart coordinate $x^a$ has unit metre and $x^0=ct$.

[L2] [[def-em-si-conventions]]: $\mu_0$ carries $\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is measured, while $e_{\rm SI}$ and $c$ have exact SI defining values.

[L3] [[def-em-si-conventions]]: the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $\mathbf A$ carries T m, so the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ carry T m.

[L4] [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]: the covariant components are $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$.

[L5] [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]: when a $C^1$ potential $A_\mu$ is supplied, $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$.

## Proof

1.1 Since each coordinate has unit metre by [L1], each coordinate derivative has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. With $m_{\rm rest,SI}$ in kg, $c$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $\hbar$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$, the quotient $m_{\rm rest,SI}c/\hbar$ has unit $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})/(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}})=\mathrm m^{-1}$. Therefore $|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $\omega_\mu$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\hbar c\omega_\mu$ has unit J, and $\hbar\mathbf k$ has unit $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. [given, L1, A1, algebra]

1.2 The SI four-potential has unit $\mathrm{T\,m}$ by [L3], which equals $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}\,A^{-1}}$. From [L2] and [A1], $\mu_0\hbar c$ has unit $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}\,A^{-2}})(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}) (\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})=\mathrm{kg^2\,m^4\,s^{-4}\,A^{-2}}$; its positive square root has unit $\mathrm{J\,A^{-1}}$. Thus $a^\mu$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. By [L5], differentiating the potential with a length-coordinate derivative gives $F_{\rm SI}$ unit $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}\,A^{-1}}$; division by $\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ gives $f^{\mu\nu}$ unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$. The $F$-component unit is consistent with $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ in [L4]. [given, L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, A1, algebra]

1.3 Using $\mu_0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}\,A^{-2}}$, the quantity $\mu_0c/\hbar$ has unit $\mathrm{A^{-2}\,s^{-2}}=\mathrm{C^{-2}}$ by [A1]. Hence $q_{\rm n}$ and $e_{\rm n}$ are dimensionless, as is $\alpha=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Both $\partial_\mu$ and $q_{\rm n}a_\mu$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, so the terms in $D_\mu$ are dimensionally compatible. If $q_{\rm SI}=0$, then $q_{\rm n}=0$ and the same expression reduces to $D_\mu=\partial_\mu$, so the zero-charge case is also well-defined. [given, L2, A1, algebra]

1.4 Under [A2], the dimensionless action $S/\hbar$ is the integral of $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ against a four-volume of unit $\mathrm m^4$, so $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$. Multiplication by $\hbar c$, of unit $\mathrm{J\,m}$, gives the SI Lagrangian density $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SI}}$ with unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. [given, A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 Write $d_L(X)$ for the exponent of metre in the engineering dimension of $X$. By [L1], $d_L(\partial_a)=-1$. The scalar kinetic density in [A2] has degree $2(d_L(\phi_{\rm n})-1)$; equating it to $-4$ gives $d_L(\phi_{\rm n})=-1$. The Dirac kinetic density has degree $d_L(\bar\psi)+d_L(\psi)-1$; the equality $d_L(\bar\psi)=d_L(\psi)$ in [A2] and density degree $-4$ give $d_L(\psi_{\rm n})=-3/2$. The photon kinetic density gives $2(d_L(a)-1)=-4$, hence $d_L(a)=-1$ and, since $f$ has one derivative of $a$, $d_L(f)=-2$. These are precisely the stated canonical engineering degrees. [given, L1, A2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation

$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

## Statement

Fix an inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] and identify its vector coordinates with $\mathbb R^4$ and $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi\in\mathbb R$, define the boost $B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)$ by $B e_0=\cosh\chi\,e_0+\sinh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, $B\mathbf n_B=\sinh\chi\,e_0+\cosh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, and $Bw=w$ for every $w$ Euclidean-orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n_B)$. Every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]], admits $\Lambda=B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$, where $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ fixes the time axis and $\mathbf n_R$, and sends $\mathbf v_\perp$ to $\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n_R\times\mathbf v_\perp$ on the orthogonal plane, where $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$; the cross product is [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. If $\Lambda e_0=e_0$, choose $\chi=0$ and $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)=\Lambda$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model, the inertial orthonormal frame, and the proper orthochronous Lorentz group.

[F1] The metric in the selected inertial basis is $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and the first basis vector $e_0$ is future unit timelike. [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]

[F2] A proper orthochronous Lorentz map preserves $\eta_0$, has determinant $+1$, and preserves the chosen future timelike component; moreover these maps form a group under composition, including closure under inverse, by [[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]] and the definition in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]. In the selected inertial coordinates this is the group denoted $SO^+(1,3)$.

[F3] The hyperbolic functions satisfy $\cosh^2\chi-\sinh^2\chi=1$, $\cosh$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$ on $[0,\infty)$, and $\sinh$ is odd and strictly increasing; the intermediate value theorem applies to real polynomials. [[def-hyperbolic-functions]] [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]] [[thm-intermediate-value]]

[F4] Every point $(a,b)$ with $a^2+b^2=1$ has the form $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ for some real $\theta$. [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]

[F5] Cauchy--Schwarz gives $|\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_B|\le|\mathbf v|$ for unit $\mathbf n_B$. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]

[F6] From the definitions, $\cosh\chi-\sinh\chi=\exp(-\chi)>0$. [[def-hyperbolic-functions]] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F7] Spatial vectors use the Euclidean inner product and the right-handed cross product; for orthogonal unit vectors $\mathbf n,\mathbf f$, the coordinate definition gives $\mathbf n\times\mathbf f$ unit and orthogonal to both. [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]

## Proof

**Given:** The assumptions and geometric structure in [F1]–[F6].

1.1 Let $u=\Lambda e_0=(u^0,\mathbf u)$. By [F1]–[F2], $u^0>0$ and $-(u^0)^2+|\mathbf u|^2=-1$, so $u^0=\sqrt{1+|\mathbf u|^2}$. If $\mathbf u=0$, then $u=e_0$; choose any unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi=0$, so $B_{\mathbf n_B}(0)=I$. Otherwise $\mathbf n_B=\mathbf u/|\mathbf u|$ is a unit vector and $u^0>1$. By the range and strict increase in [F3], there is a unique $\chi>0$ with $\cosh\chi=u^0$; then $\sinh\chi>0$ and $\sinh^2\chi=(u^0)^2-1=|\mathbf u|^2$, so $\sinh\chi=|\mathbf u|$. Define $B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)$ by the block $\begin{pmatrix}\cosh\chi&\sinh\chi\\\sinh\chi&\cosh\chi\end{pmatrix}$ on $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n_B)$ and the identity on its Euclidean orthogonal complement. The hyperbolic identity in [F3] verifies metric preservation and the block determinant is $1$. For a future timelike $v=(v^0,\mathbf v)$, the signature gives $v^0>|\mathbf v|$, and [F5] gives $|\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_B|\le|\mathbf v|$. Hence $v'^{0}=\cosh\chi\,v^0+\sinh\chi(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_B)\ge(\cosh\chi-\sinh\chi)v^0>0$ by [F6]. Thus $B\in SO^+(1,3)$ and $Be_0=u$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, given, construct]

2.1 Set $R=B^{-1}\Lambda$. Since both $B$ by step 1.1 and $\Lambda$ by hypothesis belong to the proper orthochronous Lorentz group, its inverse and composition closure in [F2] give $R\in SO^+(1,3)$; also $Re_0=e_0$. If $v$ is spatial, then $\eta_0(Rv,e_0)=\eta_0(Rv,Re_0)=\eta_0(v,e_0)=0$, so $R$ preserves the spatial orthogonal complement. Its restriction $Q$ there is an orthogonal $3\times3$ matrix with determinant $+1$ because $\det R=1$ and its time block is $1$. Hence $Q\in SO(3)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The real polynomial $p(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I_3-Q)$ is continuous (it is a finite sum of products of affine functions) and has opposite signs for sufficiently large positive and negative $\lambda$, since its leading term is $\lambda^3$. The intermediate value theorem [F3] gives a real eigenvalue $\lambda$. Orthogonality implies $|\lambda|=1$, so $\lambda=\pm1$. If $-1$ is the only real eigenvalue and the other two eigenvalues are nonreal, they are a conjugate pair whose product is positive; then $\det Q=-1$, contrary to $\det Q=1$. If all eigenvalues are real, their product $1$ means the number of $-1$ eigenvalues is even, so at least one eigenvalue is $+1$. Thus $Q$ has a unit fixed vector $\mathbf n_R$. Choose a standard spatial basis vector $e_j$ not parallel to $\mathbf n_R$ (one exists because the spatial basis spans $\mathbb R^3$), and set $f_1=(e_j-(e_j\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R)/|e_j-(e_j\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R|$ and $f_2=\mathbf n_R\times f_1$. By [F7], $f_1,f_2$ are an orthonormal basis of $\mathbf n_R^\perp$. The restriction of $Q$ to this plane is orthogonal with determinant $+1$, so in this basis its matrix has form $\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}$ with $a^2+b^2=1$. By [F4] there is $\theta$ with $a=\cos\theta$, $b=\sin\theta$. Therefore $Q$ is the rotation $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ about $\mathbf n_R$. [F2, F3, F4, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The spatial restriction of $R$ is the rotation from step 3.1, so $R=R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ on all of $\mathbb R^4$ because $Re_0=e_0$. Since $\Lambda=BR$, this is the required boost-rotation factorization. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and use the definitions in [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]. For every $\mu\ge0$ and almost every $\mathbf k$, the displayed Pauli blocks satisfy $h_D(\mathbf k)^\dagger=h_D(\mathbf k)$, $h_D(\mathbf k)^2=\omega(\mathbf k)^2I_4$, and $P_\pm(\mathbf k)$ are complementary orthogonal projections of rank two. The ranges $\mathcal H_\pm$ are closed separable Hilbert subspaces of $\mathcal H_D$, and $h_D$ is self-adjoint on $D(h_D)=\{u:\omega u\in\mathcal H_D\}$. The matrices also satisfy $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ and $\gamma^{0\dagger}=\gamma^0$, $\gamma^{j\dagger}=-\gamma^j$.

For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n$, put $\Sigma_{\mathbf n}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf n,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf n)$, $S_R(\theta)=\cos(\theta/2)I_4-i\sin(\theta/2)\Sigma_{\mathbf n}$, and $S_B(\chi)=\cosh(\chi/2)I_4+\sinh(\chi/2)\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf n$. With $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$ the rotation $\mathbf v_\parallel+\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n\times\mathbf v_\perp$ using [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], with $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$, and $B_{\mathbf n}(\chi)$ the boost defined in [[lem-qft-lorentz-boost-rotation-factorization]], these matrices satisfy $S_R\Gamma(p)S_R^{-1}=\Gamma(R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)p)$, $S_B\Gamma(p)S_B^{-1}=\Gamma(B_{\mathbf n}(\chi)p)$, and $S_R\beta S_R^\dagger=S_B\beta S_B^\dagger=\beta$.

For each real $t$, $W_D(t,\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] is unitary, satisfies $W_D(t+s,\mathbf k)=W_D(t,\mathbf k)W_D(s,\mathbf k)$, and obeys $\partial_tW_D(t,\mathbf k)=i h_D(\mathbf k)W_D(t,\mathbf k)$.

Thus $\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I_2$. The block formulas then give $\alpha_i^\dagger=\alpha_i$, $\beta^\dagger=\beta$, $\alpha_i\alpha_j+\alpha_j\alpha_i=2\delta_{ij}I_4$, and $\alpha_i\beta+\beta\alpha_i=0$. Consequently $h_D^\dagger=h_D$ and $h_D^2=(|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2)I_4=\omega^2I_4$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Where $\omega>0$, the self-adjoint matrix $h_D/\omega$ squares to $I_4$. Hence $P_\pm^\dagger=P_\pm$, $P_\pm^2=P_\pm$, $P_+P_-=0$, and $P_++P_-=I_4$. Since $\operatorname{tr}(h_D)=0$, $\operatorname{tr}(P_\pm)=2$; a finite-dimensional orthogonal projection has eigenvalues only $0,1$, so its trace equals its rank and each rank is two. The chosen values at the massless apex have the same projection and rank properties. The matrix fields are measurable and have operator norm at most one, so their multiplication operators are bounded everywhere-defined projections; their ranges are closed and give $\mathcal H_D=\mathcal H_+\oplus\mathcal H_-$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\mathcal R$ be the countable real rational-box family from [F3].
