Therefore $h_D=T_+\oplus T_-$ is self-adjoint on $\{u:\omega u\in\mathcal H_D\}$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For $\omega>0$, write $W_D(t)=\cos(\omega t)I+i\sin(\omega t)h_D/\omega$. Using $h_D^2=\omega^2I$ and $h_D^\dagger=h_D$ from step 1.1, the product $W_D(t)^\dagger W_D(t)=(\cos^2(\omega t)+\sin^2(\omega t))I=I$. The sine and cosine addition formulas give $W_D(t+s)=W_D(t)W_D(s)$, and differentiating gives $\partial_t W_D=i h_D W_D$. At the massless apex the assigned value is the identity and does not affect the multiplication operator. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces,
let $\overline{\mu\times\nu}$ be their completed product measure, and put
$H_X=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ and $H_Y=L^2(Y,\nu;\mathbb C)$ with the
second-variable-linear pairing fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. There is a unique unitary

$$T:H_X\widehat\otimes H_Y\longrightarrow L^2(X\times Y,\overline{\mu\times\nu};\mathbb C)$$

whose value on each elementary tensor is
$T(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ almost everywhere. In particular, the Hilbert
tensor completion is identified with the full product $L^2$ space, not only
with the closure of a chosen class of product functions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; sigma-finite measure spaces $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$
and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$; their completed product measure; and the quotient
$L^2$ spaces with their integral pairings.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the premise used by the completed-product
measure and Hilbert tensor suppliers. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The product measure is sigma-finite and satisfies
$(\mu\times\nu)(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B)$ on measurable rectangles; its
completion changes measurable sets only by subsets of product-null sets.
[[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]
[[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]
[[def-completed-product-measure]]
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F2] Tonelli's theorem computes integrals of nonnegative product functions,
and Fubini's theorem identifies product integrals of integrable functions
with either iterated integral.
[[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]

[F7] Cauchy–Schwarz holds in each $L^2$ space, so products of two $L^2$
functions on the same factor are integrable.
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]

[F3] Simple functions with finite-measure support are dense in $L^2$.
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]
[[thm-simple-functions-with-finite-measure-support-are-dense-in-l-p-for-finite-p]]

[F4] The product sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles; these
rectangles form a pi-system, and a lambda-system containing a generating
pi-system contains its generated sigma-algebra.
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]
[[def-measurable-rectangle]]
[[def-pi-system]]
[[def-lambda-system]]
[[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]

[F5] The tensor inner product on elementary tensors is the product pairing and
their finite linear span is dense in the Hilbert tensor completion.
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]

[F6] For increasing measurable sets, measure is continuous from below.
[[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]

## Proof

1.1 Measurable representatives may be chosen for $f,f',g,g'$. Replacing a
representative on a null set changes its product only on a product-null set:
cover the other sigma-finite factor by countably many finite-measure sets and
apply the rectangle formula [F1] on each. Thus the product rule is well
defined on $L^2$ classes. By [F7], $f\overline{f'}$ and $g\overline{g'}$
are integrable; Fubini [F2] gives the product norm
$\|f(x)g(y)\|_2^2=\|f\|_2^2\|g\|_2^2$, so each elementary product belongs
to the target space. It also gives
$$\langle f(x)g(y),f'(x)g'(y)\rangle_{L^2(X\times Y)} =\langle f,f'\rangle_{H_X}\langle g,g'\rangle_{H_Y}.$$
By sesquilinearity, the rule $\sum_j\alpha_j f_j\otimes g_j\mapsto
\sum_j\alpha_j f_j(x)g_j(y)$ preserves inner products on finite sums. If two
tensor presentations define the same algebraic tensor, their difference has
zero tensor norm by [F5], hence its product function has zero $L^2$ norm; the
rule is well-defined on the algebraic tensor product and extends uniquely as
an isometry $T$ to the completion. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F7, algebra]

2.1 Choose sigma-finite exhaustions $X_k\uparrow X$ and $Y_k\uparrow Y$ with finite measure, and put $Z_k=X_k\times Y_k$. By the rectangle formula [F1], $(\mu\times\nu)(Z_k)<\infty$, and $Z_k\uparrow X\times Y$. For fixed $k$, let $\mathcal C_k$ be the family of product-measurable $E\subseteq Z_k$ such that $\mathbf1_E$ belongs to the closed range of $T$. It contains $Z_k$, since $\mathbf1_{Z_k}=T(\mathbf1_{X_k}\otimes\mathbf1_{Y_k})$. If $E\subseteq F$ are in $\mathcal C_k$, then $\mathbf1_{F\setminus E}=\mathbf1_F-\mathbf1_E$ is in that closed range. If $E_j\uparrow E$ in $Z_k$, then $\|\mathbf1_E-\mathbf1_{E_j}\|_2^2=(\mu\times\nu)(E\setminus E_j)\to0$ by [F6], so $E\in\mathcal C_k$. Thus $\mathcal C_k$ is a lambda-system on $Z_k$. For every measurable rectangle $A\times B$, its restriction to $Z_k$ is $(A\cap X_k)\times(B\cap Y_k)$, whose indicator is the image of $\mathbf1_{A\cap X_k}\otimes\mathbf1_{B\cap Y_k}$; these restricted rectangles are a generating pi-system by [F4]. Dynkin's theorem [F4] gives $\mathbf1_E\in\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$ for every product-measurable $E\subseteq Z_k$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $E$ be any completed-product-measurable set with finite product measure. By the completion definition [F1], it differs from a product-measurable set $E_0$ by a subset of a product-null set, so $\mathbf1_E=\mathbf1_{E_0}$ as $L^2$ classes. Since $Z_k\uparrow X\times Y$, [F6] gives $(\mu\times\nu)(E_0\setminus Z_k)\to0$, so $\mathbf1_{E_0}=\lim_k\mathbf1_{E_0\cap Z_k}$ in $L^2$; step 2.1 puts each truncated indicator in the closed range of $T$. Every finite-measure simple function for the completed measure is a finite linear combination of indicators of completed-measurable finite-measure sets; replacing each set by its product-measurable representative gives the same $L^2$ class. Such simple functions are dense by [F3]. Consequently the range of $T$ is dense in the full target $L^2$ space. Since the range of an isometry from a complete space is closed, $T$ is onto and therefore unitary. Its uniqueness follows because elementary tensors span a dense subspace. [F1, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and use [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] and [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]]. Define $\chi(s)=\cos s+i\sin s$ for real $s$, using [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. Let $X=(\{+\}\times\mathbb R^3)\sqcup(\{-\}\times\mathbb R^3)$ carry counting measure on the species label and $d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$ on each copy. The fiber $\mathcal V_x$ is $\mathbb C^4$ for $x=(+,\mathbf k)$ and $\overline{\mathbb C^4}$ for $x=(-,\mathbf k)$; $L^2(X;\mathcal V)$ denotes measurable sections with square-integrable fiber norm, and is the direct sum $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)\oplus L^2(\mathbb R^3;\overline{\mathbb C^4})$. Identify $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ with the closed subspace whose $+$ fibers lie in $\operatorname{ran}P_+(\mathbf k)$ and whose $-$ fibers lie in $\overline{\operatorname{ran}P_-(\mathbf k)}$; form its antisymmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$ using [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. For $x=(+,\mathbf k)$ set $q(x)=(\omega(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)$, and for $x=(-,\mathbf k)$ set $q(x)=(\omega(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. The one-particle translation multipliers $V(a)u(x)=\chi(q^0(x)a^0-\mathbf q(x)\cdot\mathbf a)u(x)$ preserve $\mathcal K$ and lift to a strongly continuous unitary representation on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$. Write $U_j(t)$ for its Fock lift along the $j$th coordinate axis of $\mathbb R^4$.

On the $n$-particle sector, let $s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n q(x_r)$ and set $s_0=0$ on the vacuum sector. The joint spectral measure is multiplication by $\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}$ on each sector, restricted to its antisymmetric subspace. Its support is contained in the closed future cone $\{(E,\mathbf p):E\ge|\mathbf p|\}$. Define the time generator $H$ and spatial momentum components $P_j$ by $U(te_0)=\chi(tH)$ and $U(te_j)=\chi(-tP_j)$, where $e_\alpha$ are the coordinate vectors in translation space. Then $H$ and each $P_j$ are the maximal real multipliers by $s_{n,0}$ and $s_{n,j}$, respectively, with domains $\{\Psi:\sum_n\|s_{n,\alpha}\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$; the minus sign in spatial translation phases is the Minkowski pairing convention in $V(a)$. The vacuum is the unique zero-energy vector; for $\mu>0$ the nonvacuum spectrum has gap at least $\mu$, while for $\mu=0$ it has no positive gap.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the two closed energy subspaces and their measure conventions; antisymmetric Fock sectors; and the exact product-tensor and spectral-measure definitions.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the QFT Fock construction. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] $\omega^2=|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2$, the projections $P_\pm$ are complementary orthogonal projections, and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}P_\pm$ are closed. [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]]

[F2] The fermionic Fock space is the square-summable direct sum of antisymmetric tensor sectors; the vacuum is sector zero. [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]

[F3] The completed tensor powers are identified with product $L^2$ spaces, and the antisymmetric sector is the range of the signed permutation average. [[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]] [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]

[F4] The joint projection-valued measure and maximal self-adjoint multiplication-domain terms use the definitions in [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]], and [[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]].

[F5] Dominated convergence applies on the completed product measures and countable direct sum used below. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F6] Sine and cosine are defined by power series, have unit-circle norm, obey the addition formulas, and have their usual derivatives; Fatou's lemma applies to nonnegative squared difference quotients. [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]] [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] [[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F7] The Euclidean norm obeys the triangle inequality. [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]

## Proof



1.1 Realize the one-particle space as the closed subspace of the direct sum $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)\oplus L^2(\mathbb R^3;\overline{\mathbb C^4})$ determined by $P_+$ and $\overline{P_-}$. In each fiber, $|\chi(s)|^2=\cos^2s+\sin^2s=1$ by [F6], so the phase multiplier preserves norms and both projected ranges. The addition formulas give $\chi(s+t)=\chi(s)\chi(t)$, hence $V(a)V(b)=V(a+b)$. [F1, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 If $a_m\to a$, the multiplier phases converge pointwise by continuity of sine and cosine, and the squared difference applied to any $u\in\mathcal K$ is bounded by $4|u|^2$. Dominated convergence [F5] gives $\|V(a_m)u-V(a)u\|\to0$. On an elementary $n$-fold tensor, the difference of $V(a)^{\otimes n}$ and $V(b)^{\otimes n}$ is a sum of $n$ terms, each with one factor $(V(a)-V(b))u_r$ and all other factors of unchanged norm. Thus strong continuity holds on elementary tensors, then on each completed antisymmetric sector by density and the unit norm bound. Finite-sector truncations are dense in Fock space, so the direct-sum lift is strongly continuous on all of $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The ambient one-particle space has two species and four complex fiber coordinates per species, so it is the finite orthogonal sum of eight scalar $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ spaces. Distributing a finite $n$-fold Hilbert tensor over this sum gives a finite orthogonal sum indexed by the $n$ species/fiber-coordinate choices; applying the scalar product-tensor identification [F3] successively identifies each summand with scalar $L^2((\mathbb R^3)^n)$. The projected space $\mathcal K^{\widehat\otimes n}$ is a closed subspace of this product space, and its antisymmetric sector is the range of the signed permutation average. The function $s_n$ is measurable and permutation-invariant. Therefore multiplication by $\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}$ preserves that sector and is an orthogonal projection. The direct sum over $n$, with vacuum multiplier $\mathbf1_B(0)$, satisfies $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$ and $E(\mathbb R^4)=I$. For disjoint $B_m$ with union $B$, the squared norm of the difference between $E(B)\Psi$ and $\sum_{m=0}^N E(B_m)\Psi$ is the integral of $|\Psi|^2$ over the decreasing remainder preimages; the indicators tend pointwise to zero and are bounded by one, so [F5] gives norm convergence. Hence $E$ is a strongly countably additive projection-valued measure. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Fix one real coordinate multiplier $s_{n,j}$ on an antisymmetric sector. It is finite, measurable, real, and permutation-invariant. Its maximal domain is dense because the cutoffs $\Psi_n\mathbf1_{\{|s_{n,j}|\le N\}}$ are antisymmetric domain vectors converging in norm by [F5]; multiplication is symmetric because $s_{n,j}$ is real. If $\Psi_n$ is in the adjoint domain with adjoint value $Q_n$, then $v_N=(s_{n,j}\Psi_n-Q_n)\mathbf1_{\{|s_{n,j}|\le N\}}$ is antisymmetric and in the maximal domain. The adjoint identity gives $0=\langle s_{n,j}v_N,\Psi_n\rangle-\langle v_N,Q_n\rangle=\int_{\{|s_{n,j}|\le N\}}|s_{n,j}\Psi_n-Q_n|^2$. Letting $N\to\infty$ proves $Q_n=s_{n,j}\Psi_n\in L^2$; the converse adjoint inclusion follows from the same real-multiplier identity. Thus each sector multiplier is self-adjoint on its maximal domain. [F4, F5, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The direct-sum multiplier $A_j=\bigoplus_n M_{s_{n,j}}$ is symmetric on the displayed domain. If $\Psi$ belongs to $D(A_j^*)$ with adjoint value $Q$, testing the adjoint identity against vectors supported in one sector shows $\Psi_n\in D(M_{s_{n,j}}^*)$ and $(A_j^*\Psi)_n=M_{s_{n,j}}^*\Psi_n=s_{n,j}\Psi_n$, by step 3.1. Since $Q$ is in the Fock direct sum, $\sum_n\|s_{n,j}\Psi_n\|^2=\sum_n\|Q_n\|^2<\infty$, so $\Psi\in D(A_j)$. Conversely, if $\Psi\in D(A_j)$, sectorwise symmetry and Cauchy--Schwarz for the square-summable sector sequences give $\langle A_j\Phi,\Psi\rangle=\langle\Phi,A_j\Psi\rangle$ for every $\Phi\in D(A_j)$; hence $\Psi\in D(A_j^*)$ with $A_j^*\Psi=A_j\Psi$. Therefore $A_j=A_j^*$ with exactly the stated domain. Truncating both particle number and the multiplier to bounded level sets approximates each domain vector in graph norm by [F5], so finite-sector domain vectors form a graph core. [F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For every point of $X$, $q^0=\omega\ge|\mathbf q|$ by [F1]. For any finite list $q_1,\ldots,q_n$, the time component of their sum is nonnegative and $|\sum_r\mathbf q_r|\le\sum_r|\mathbf q_r|\le\sum_rq_r^0$ by [F7]. Thus every $s_n$ lies in the closed future cone, including $s_0=0$, so the spectral measure from step 2.2 is supported there. If $\mu>0$, then $s_{n,0}\ge n\mu\ge\mu$ for $n\ge1$. If $\mu=0$, $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$ except at the Lebesgue-null point $\mathbf k=0$; consequently $s_{n,0}>0$ almost everywhere on every $n\ge1$ product sector and the zero-energy projection has only the vacuum range. [F1, F4, F7, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $\mu=0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\mathbf k_0$ with $0<|\mathbf k_0|<\varepsilon/4$. Since $P_+(\mathbf k_0)$ has rank two, choose $e\in\mathbb C^4$ with $P_+(\mathbf k_0)e\ne0$. Continuity of $P_+$ away from the origin gives a bounded open ball $B$ about $\mathbf k_0$, with closure avoiding zero and contained in $\{|\mathbf k|<\varepsilon/2\}$, on which $P_+(\mathbf k)e\ne0$. The measurable function $u=\mathbf1_B P_+e$ is square-integrable, nonzero, and supported where $0<\omega<\varepsilon$. Hence the one-particle spectral measure has nonzero mass below every $\varepsilon>0$, so there is no positive massless gap. [F1, F4, step 4.2, construct]

6.1 For real $r$, the mean value theorem and $|\cos s|\le1$ from [F6] give $|\sin r|\le|r|$, hence $|\chi(r)-1|=2|\sin(r/2)|\le|r|$. Also $\chi'(r)=i\chi(r)$ by the sine and cosine derivative formulas. For a coordinate translation set $\varepsilon_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_j=-1$ for $j=1,2,3$, and write $U_\alpha(t)=U(te_\alpha)$; on each sector this is multiplication by $\chi(\varepsilon_\alpha t s_{n,\alpha})$ by the definition of $V(a)$. If $\Psi$ is in the maximal multiplication domain, then $|(\chi(\varepsilon_\alpha t s_{n,\alpha})-1)/t|\le|s_{n,\alpha}|$; dominated convergence [F5] makes the norm derivative equal $i\varepsilon_\alpha s_{n,\alpha}\Psi$. Conversely, if the difference quotient has a norm limit, take $t_m=1/m$. Pointwise the quotient tends to $i\varepsilon_\alpha s_{n,\alpha}\Psi_n$, so Fatou's lemma [F6] gives $\sum_n\|s_{n,\alpha}\Psi_n\|^2\le\liminf_m\|(U_\alpha(t_m)-I)\Psi/t_m\|^2<\infty$. Thus the derivative domain is exactly the displayed maximal domain; the self-adjoint generator with convention $U(te_0)=\chi(tH)$ or $U(te_j)=\chi(-tP_j)$ is the multiplier $s_{n,\alpha}$. Applying the same argument to $a\mapsto U(ta)$ gives the maximal multiplier by $a^0s_{n,0}-\sum_j a^js_{n,j}$ for any real $a$. [F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space, with separability taken in its Hilbert norm topology
as defined in [[def-separable-space]], and with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a separable complex Hilbert space $H$; the
symmetric and antisymmetric sectors, finite-particle domain, creation and
annihilation formulas from [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the only choice principle assumed by the
Hilbert tensor suppliers used below. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Completed Hilbert tensor products use the product inner product, and
elementary tensors have dense span.
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]

[F2] Permutations act unitarily on each tensor power; the averaging operators
$P_{s,n}$ and $P_{a,n}$ are orthogonal projections onto the symmetric and
antisymmetric sectors.
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]

[F3] The sector creation, annihilation, and contraction maps are given by the
formulas in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]: creation inserts $h$ and applies
the symmetric or antisymmetric projection with the factor $\sqrt{n+1}$;
annihilation contracts the first factor with $C_h$ and the factor $\sqrt n$.

[F4] A bounded map $S$ induces $S\otimes I$ on a completed tensor product
with norm at most $\|S\|$; orthogonal complements use the Hilbert orthogonality
convention. [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]
[[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]

[F5] The graph norm, closedness, core and adjoint-domain terms have the
definitions in [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], and
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]].

## Proof

1.1 Each sector $H_s^{(n)}$ or $H_a^{(n)}$ is a closed subspace of its Hilbert tensor power, being the range of the corresponding orthogonal projection [F2]. The square-summable direct sum of these sectors is complete: for a Cauchy sequence, each coordinate converges in its complete sector; finite partial sums of squared coordinate norms are bounded by the common sequence bound, so the coordinate limits are square-summable; taking coordinate limits in the Cauchy estimate over each finite set of coordinates and then the supremum proves convergence in the direct-sum norm. Truncating a square-summable sequence after sector $N$ converges in norm, so $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense. [A1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

1.2 On sector $n$, creation and contraction have norms at most $\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|$ and $\sqrt n\|h\|$, respectively: the contraction has norm at most $\|h\|$ on its first factor by Cauchy–Schwarz and extends to the tensor product with the same bound [F4]; each symmetrizer or antisymmetrizer has norm at most one [F2]. For $\Phi\in H_s^{(n)}$ and $\Psi\in H_s^{(n+1)}$, use $P_{s,n+1}\Psi=\Psi$ and self-adjointness of $P_{s,n+1}$ to compute $\langle a_n^\dagger(h)\Phi,\Psi\rangle_2 =\sqrt{n+1}\langle h\otimes\Phi,\Psi\rangle_2 =\sqrt{n+1}\langle\Phi,(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes n})\Psi\rangle_2 =\langle\Phi,a_{n+1}(h)\Psi\rangle_2$; the tensor product pairing gives the middle equality because $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$. The same calculation with $P_{a,n+1}$ proves the fermionic relation. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The maximal bosonic direct-sum maps are closed. For example, if $\Phi^{(j)}\to\Phi$ and $a(h)\Phi^{(j)}\to\Theta$ in Fock norm, boundedness of each sector map gives coordinatewise $\Theta_{n-1}=a_n(h)\Phi_n$; since $\Theta$ is square-summable, the defining sum for $D(a(h))$ is finite and $a(h)\Phi=\Theta$. The same coordinate argument applies to $a^\dagger(h)$. Truncating a vector and its image after sector $N$ shows $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a graph core for each. For the adjoint, testing against vectors supported in input sector $n$ forces the output coordinate in sector $n+1$ to be $a_{n+1}^\dagger(h)\Phi_n$; square-summability of these coordinates is exactly the displayed domain of $a^\dagger(h)$. Conversely, if that sum is finite, the sector pairing of step 1.2 and Cauchy–Schwarz in the direct sum give the adjoint identity for every vector in $D(a(h))$. Thus $a(h)^*=a^\dagger(h)$ with the displayed maximal domains. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

2.2 For a symmetric elementary tensor $v_1\vee\cdots\vee v_n:=P_{s,n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, contraction and creation give $a(h)(v_1\vee\cdots\vee v_n)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^n\langle h,v_j\rangle_2 \,v_1\vee\cdots\widehat{v_j}\cdots\vee v_n$ and $a^\dagger(k)(v_1\vee\cdots\vee v_n)=\sqrt{n+1}\, P_{s,n+1}(k\otimes v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, by expanding the permutation averages [F2]. In the composition $a(h)a^\dagger(k)$, the contraction term for the newly inserted $k$ is $\langle h,k\rangle_2(v_1\vee\cdots\vee v_n)$; each of the other $n$ contraction terms is exactly the corresponding term of $a^\dagger(k)a(h)$. Hence their difference is $\langle h,k\rangle_2I$. Symmetry of $P_{s,n}$ makes two creations commute; two contractions commute because contracting distinct tensor slots in either order gives the same sum. Finite elementary symmetric tensors are dense in each sector and the sector maps are bounded there, so the identities hold on all of $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For a unit vector $h$, put $K=h^\perp$. In the $n$th antisymmetric sector, every $v\in H$ decomposes as $v=\langle h,v\rangle_2h+(v-\langle h,v\rangle_2h)$ with the second term in $K$, so $H=\mathbb Ch\oplus K$. Tensors split orthogonally into those with no $h$ factor and those with exactly one: expand each tensor factor in $\mathbb Ch\oplus K$; terms with two $h$ factors vanish under antisymmetrization, and different placements of the single $h$ are orthogonal. The map $\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\cdot)$ is an isometry from the no-$h$ part of sector $n$ onto the one-$h$ part of sector $n+1$, since the $n+1$ placements are orthogonal and each has coefficient $1/(n+1)$ in the antisymmetrizer. It vanishes on the one-$h$ part. Its adjoint $c(h)$ reverses this isometry and vanishes on the no-$h$ part. Thus $c(h)c^\dagger(h)+c^\dagger(h)c(h)=I$ and both maps have norm one. Scaling gives $\{c(h),c^\dagger(h)\}=\|h\|^2I$ and norms $\|h\|$ for $h\ne0$; for $h=0$ these statements hold because both operators vanish. Antisymmetry gives $c^\dagger(h)^2=0$; taking adjoints gives $c(h)^2=0$. Polarizing the diagonal anticommutator at $h+k$ and $h+ik$, using that $c(\cdot)$ is conjugate-linear and $c^\dagger(\cdot)$ is linear, yields $\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I$: if $q(u)=\{c(u),c^\dagger(u)\}$, then the sesquilinear polarization identity is $B(h,k)=\tfrac14(q(h+k)-q(h-k)-i q(h+ik)+i q(h-ik))$, where $B(h,k)=\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}$; substituting $q(u)=\|u\|^2I$ gives the claimed scalar. Polarizing $c(u)^2=0$ and $c^\dagger(u)^2=0$ gives the two same-type anticommutators. All fermionic maps are bounded, so these identities hold on the whole Fock space. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ and $K$ be complex
Hilbert spaces and let $U:H\to K$ be unitary. The sector maps
$U^{\otimes n}$ restrict to unitaries $U_s^{(n)}:H_s^{(n)}\to K_s^{(n)}$;
their direct sum
$$\Gamma_s(U)=\bigoplus_{n=0}^\infty U_s^{(n)}$$
is unitary, maps vacuum to vacuum, and maps the finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}(H)$ onto $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}(K)$. It intertwines the
creation and annihilation maps:
$$\Gamma_s(U)a_H^\dagger(h)\Gamma_s(U)^{-1}=a_K^\dagger(Uh),\qquad \Gamma_s(U)a_H(h)\Gamma_s(U)^{-1}=a_K(Uh)$$
on the finite-particle domain. If $G$ is a topological space and $g\mapsto U_g$
is a family of unitaries such that $g\mapsto U_gh$ is norm-continuous for
every $h\in H$, then $g\mapsto\Gamma_s(U_g)$ has the same continuity
property on $\mathcal F_s(H)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the symmetric tensor-sector Fock conventions and creation/annihilation formulas of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

[A1] Countable Choice is the choice assumption used for the completed tensor and sector constructions. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Fock space is the Hilbert direct sum of symmetric tensor powers, the vacuum is the zeroth sector, finite-particle vectors are dense, and creation and annihilation are the symmetrized tensor-insertion and contraction maps. [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]

[F2] Hilbert tensor products are completed from elementary tensors, and permutation averaging is the orthogonal projection onto the symmetric subspace. [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]

## Proof

1.1 Since $U$ is unitary, $U^{\otimes n}$ is unitary on the completed tensor power by its isometric action on elementary tensors and its inverse $(U^{-1})^{\otimes n}$. It commutes with every tensor-factor permutation, because both compositions send an elementary tensor to $Uh_{\pi(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Uh_{\pi(n)}$. It therefore commutes with the symmetric averaging projection of [F2] and restricts to a unitary $U_s^{(n)}$ on its range. The zeroth sector is the identity on $\mathbb C$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The direct sum of the sector unitaries preserves the sum of squared sector norms and has inverse $\bigoplus_n(U^{-1})_s^{(n)}$, so it is unitary. It fixes the zeroth-sector vacuum and preserves finite sums of sectors in both directions. On an elementary symmetric tensor, applying the Fock creation formula before or after this direct sum gives the symmetrization of $Uh$ together with the images of the original tensor factors; hence the two creation maps intertwine. The annihilation formula is its adjoint contraction and the same tensor calculation replaces each contracted vector $h$ by $Uh$. Linearity, boundedness on each fixed sector, and density of elementary tensors extend both identities to $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Fix $n$. For an elementary tensor,
$$\|U_g^{\otimes n}(h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_n) -U_{g_0}^{\otimes n}(h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_n)\| \le\sum_{r=1}^n\prod_{s\ne r}\|h_s\|\, \|(U_g-U_{g_0})h_r\|,$$
by the telescoping expansion of the tensor difference and unitary norm
preservation. Strong continuity of $U_g$ makes the right side tend to zero.
Density of elementary tensors and the uniform norm bound $1$ extend
continuity to the completed sector and its closed symmetric subspace. Finite
sector sums are dense by [F1]; approximating an arbitrary Fock vector by
such a sum and using $\|\Gamma_s(U_g)\|=1$ proves strong continuity on the
whole direct sum. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every $\mu\ge0$, the measure $d\nu_\mu$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is locally finite and sigma-finite on $H_\mu^+$.
For every proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$ and every
nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $H_\mu^+$,
$$\int_{H_\mu^+}g(\Lambda^{-1}p)\,d\nu_\mu(p) =\int_{H_\mu^+}g(p)\,d\nu_\mu(p).$$
The claim applies off the omitted apex when $\mu=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the shell parameterization, measure and metric convention of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and a proper orthochronous Lorentz map $\Lambda$.

[A1] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The shell is parameterized by $F_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)$; $-\eta(p,x)=p\circ x$ and $d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/[(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)]$. [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]

[F2] The affine Minkowski metric has signature $(-+++)$ in an inertial frame; proper orthochronous Lorentz maps preserve that form, have determinant $+1$, and preserve the chosen future timelike cone. [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]

[F3] Under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open Euclidean sets satisfies change of variables for every nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable function. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]

## Proof

1.1 On $\mathbf k\ne0$ if $\mu=0$, and on all $\mathbf k$ if $\mu>0$, $F_\mu$ is a smooth chart of the shell. On every compact subset of this chart the density $[(2\pi)^3 2\omega_\mu]^{-1}$ is bounded; for $\mu=0$ near the omitted apex it is proportional to $|\mathbf k|^{-1}$, whose integral over a radius-$r$ ball is proportional to $\int_0^r s\,ds<\infty$. Compact annuli, and for $\mu>0$ compact balls, give a countable cover by finite-measure sets; hence $d\nu_\mu$ is locally finite and sigma-finite. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\Lambda$ and write $F=F_\mu$, $F(\mathbf k')=\Lambda F(\mathbf k)$.
Because $\Lambda$ preserves the future shell, this defines a smooth
diffeomorphism $\mathbf k\mapsto\mathbf k'$ on the chart; let
$J=D\mathbf k'/D\mathbf k$. Put $q_0=(1,0,0,0)$. The columns of
$[q_0,DF(\mathbf k)]$ have determinant $1$. Differentiating
$\Lambda F(\mathbf k)=F(\mathbf k')$ gives
$\Lambda DF(\mathbf k)=DF(\mathbf k')J$, and therefore
$$1=\det[\Lambda q_0,DF(\mathbf k')]\det J.$$
For any $u\in\mathbb R^4$, direct expansion of the determinant gives
$\det[u,DF(\mathbf k')]=-\eta(u,F(\mathbf k'))/\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')$.
Take $u=\Lambda q_0$. Metric preservation and
$F(\mathbf k')=\Lambda F(\mathbf k)$ imply
$-\eta(\Lambda q_0,F(\mathbf k'))=-\eta(q_0,F(\mathbf k))
=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)$. Thus $\det J=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')/
\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)>0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The change-of-variables theorem [F3] and the Jacobian from 2.1 give
$$\frac{d^3\mathbf k'}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')} =\frac{\det J\,d^3\mathbf k}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')} =\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}.$$
For the pullback $g(\Lambda^{-1}p)$ in the Statement, apply the same
calculation to $\Lambda^{-1}$, which is again proper orthochronous.
Multiplication by the constant $[2(2\pi)^3]^{-1}$ then proves invariance for
nonnegative Borel functions. The massless apex is a
single omitted point and was never in the chart; the locally finite density
has no extra point mass there. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. For every $\mu\ge0$, the
space $H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu)$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is separable (has a countable norm-dense subset), and
$$\{K_\mu f:f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)\}$$
is dense in $H_\mu$. If $\mu>0$, the range contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$; if $\mu=0$, it contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the shell chart and Fourier restriction in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]; the listed $L^2$ density and Fourier results.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies countable dense families for the $L^2$ spaces used below. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Rational box step functions form a countable dense subset of the real-valued $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$, by [[thm-rational-box-step-functions-form-a-countable-dense-subset-of-l-p-of-rn]]

[F2] On every open subset of Euclidean space, smooth compactly supported functions are dense in its $L^2$ space. [[lem-smooth-compactly-supported-functions-are-dense-in-ltwo-of-an-open-set]]

[F3] The standard Fourier transform is a continuous automorphism of Schwartz space with a continuous inverse; composing it with the reflection and rescaling in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] gives the convention used here. [[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]

[F4] There is a smooth compactly supported bump equal to one at the origin. [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]

[F5] Integrals of increasing nonnegative measurable functions converge to the integral of their pointwise limit. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

## Proof

1.1 In the chart $\mathbf k\mapsto p_\mu(\mathbf k)$, write
$w_\mu(\mathbf k)=[2(2\pi)^3\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)]^{-1}$. By [F3] and the
fixed invertible reflection and rescaling in
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], $\mathcal F_+f$ is Schwartz for every
$f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$. Thus
$$q_2(f):=\sup_{q\in\mathbb R^4}(1+|q|)^2|\mathcal F_+f(q)|<\infty.$$
On the shell, $|\mathcal F_+f(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)|\le
q_2(f)(1+|\mathbf k|)^{-2}$, so
$$\|K_\mu f\|_{H_\mu}^2\le\frac{q_2(f)^2}{2(2\pi)^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{(1+|\mathbf k|)^{-4}}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}\,d^3\mathbf k<\infty.$$
The radial integrand is $O(r)$ near zero if $\mu=0$, $O(r^2)$ near zero if
$\mu>0$, and $O(r^{-3})$ at infinity. Therefore every $K_\mu f$ lies in
$H_\mu$, so the claimed range is a subset of the Hilbert space. By [F1],
real-valued $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ has a countable dense subset $S_{\mathbb R}$.
For complex-valued $h=u+iv\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, its real and
imaginary parts lie in real-valued $L^2$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose
$s,t\in S_{\mathbb R}$ with $\|u-s\|_2,\|v-t\|_2<\varepsilon/\sqrt2$.
Then $\|h-(s+it)\|_2^2=\|u-s\|_2^2+\|v-t\|_2^2<\varepsilon^2$.
Enumerate $S_{\mathbb R}$ by $(s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N_0}$, repeating terms if
it is finite. The Cantor pairing map
$(j,k)\mapsto (j+k)(j+k+1)/2+k$ enumerates $\mathbb N_0^2$, so
$S_{\mathbb R}+iS_{\mathbb R}$ is countable and dense in complex-valued
$L^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Multiplication by $\sqrt{w_\mu}$ is an isometry from
$H_\mu$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\},d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C)$ (for
$\mu=0$) or $L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C)$ (for $\mu>0$), with
inverse division by $\sqrt{w_\mu}$. In the massless case, extend any function
on the punctured space by zero at the null point, approximate it by the
countable dense family just constructed, and restrict those approximants back
to the punctured space; restriction does not increase the norm. Thus both
chart spaces, and therefore $H_\mu$, are separable. [A1, F1, F3, given,
algebra]

2.1 Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$ for $\mu>0$ and
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ for $\mu=0$. For
$\Omega_n=\{1/n<|\mathbf k|<n\}$, these sets increase to $\Omega\setminus\{0\}$; its complement in $\Omega$ is null for the shell measure.
For $h\in L^2(\Omega,w_\mu d^3\mathbf k)$, monotone convergence [F5] gives
$$\int_{\Omega_n}|h|^2w_\mu\,d^3\mathbf k\longrightarrow \int_\Omega|h|^2w_\mu\,d^3\mathbf k<\infty.$$
Subtracting these finite integrals from the total shows
$\|h\mathbf1_{\Omega\setminus\Omega_n}\|_{L^2(w_\mu)}\to0$.
On each $\Omega_n$, $w_\mu$ is smooth and bounded above and below by
positive constants. Approximate $h|_{\Omega_n}$ in ordinary $L^2(\Omega_n)$
by a function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega_n)$ using [F2]; equivalence of the
weighted and ordinary norms on $\Omega_n$ gives weighted approximation.
Thus $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in the shell space. [F2, F5, step 1.1,
given, algebra]

3.1 Fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Choose $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$
with $\rho(0)=1$, using [F4], and put
$$G(q^0,\mathbf q)= \psi(\mathbf q)\rho(q^0-\omega_\mu(\mathbf q)).$$
Because $\psi$ has compact support away from the massless apex, $\omega_\mu$
is smooth on a neighborhood of its support, so this is a smooth compactly
supported function on $\mathbb R^4$. By the Fourier automorphism [F3] there
is $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ with
$\mathcal F_+f(q^0,\mathbf q)=G(q^0,\mathbf q)$ in the convention of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. On the shell,
$K_\mu f(p_\mu(\mathbf k))=G(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)
=\psi(\mathbf k)$. Hence the test restriction range contains
$C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, which is dense by 2.1. [F3, F4, step 2.1, given,
construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. For every $\mu\ge0$, the
pointwise restriction
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x$$
of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] maps $\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ continuously
and linearly into $H_\mu$. It also annihilates the Klein–Gordon test operator:
$$K_\mu\bigl((\partial_0^2-\Delta+\mu^2)f\bigr)=0 \qquad(f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)).$$
The coordinates are the fixed length coordinates of that definition and
$\mu$ has inverse-length units.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the scalar shell and Fourier convention, and the
Schwartz seminorm topology.

[A1] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The shell phase is $p\circ x=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x$, and
$K_\mu f(p)=\mathcal F_+f(p)$ on $p=p_\mu(\mathbf k)$.
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]

[F2] Schwartz space consists of smooth functions whose coordinate-weighted
derivatives are bounded; these seminorms define its topology.
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]

[F3] The standard Fourier transform and inverse are continuous on Schwartz
space and are an automorphism; the reflection and rescaling in [F1] preserve
this property.
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]

[F4] For the standard Fourier convention,
Fourier transformation is continuous on Schwartz space and transforms
derivatives into polynomial multiplication, with the stated $2\pi$ factors.
After the coordinate reflection and rescaling in [F1], the same derivative
identity holds for $\mathcal F_+$.
[[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]]

## Proof

1.1 Define the continuous Schwartz seminorm
$$q_2(f)=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^4}(1+|p|)^2|\mathcal F_+f(p)|.$$
Continuity follows from [F3,F4] and [F2]. On shell,
$|\mathcal F_+f(p_\mu(\mathbf k))|
\le q_2(f)(1+|\mathbf k|)^{-2}$ because
$|p_\mu(\mathbf k)|\ge|\mathbf k|$. Hence
$$\|K_\mu f\|_{H_\mu}^2 \le\frac{q_2(f)^2}{2(2\pi)^3} \int_{\mathbb R^3} \frac{(1+|\mathbf k|)^{-4}}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
The integral is finite: in polar coordinates its radial integrand is
$r^2(1+r)^{-4}/\sqrt{r^2+\mu^2}$, which is $O(r)$ near $0$ when $\mu=0$,
is $O(r^2)$ near $0$ when $\mu>0$, and is $O(r^{-3})$ at infinity.
Therefore $K_\mu f\in H_\mu$, and the displayed seminorm bound proves
continuity and linearity. [A1,F1,F2,F3,F4,given,algebra]

2.1 By [F4], applying $\partial_0^2-\Delta+\mu^2$ before $\mathcal F_+$
multiplies by $-(p^0)^2+|\mathbf p|^2+\mu^2$. On the shell this multiplier
is $-\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)^2+|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2=0$. Restriction to the
shell therefore gives the asserted Klein–Gordon identity. [A1,F1,F4,step 1.1,given,algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the proper
orthochronous Poincare group
$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3)$ in the coordinates of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. Give $SO^+(1,3)$ the matrix subspace topology
from $M_4(\mathbb R)$ and $G$ the product topology on
$\mathbb R^4\times SO^+(1,3)$, with the group law below. A unitary
representation of this topological group is a homomorphism into the unitary
operators on $H_\mu$; it is strongly continuous when each orbit map
$g\mapsto U_\mu(g)h$ is norm-continuous for $h\in H_\mu$. For
$g=(a,\Lambda)\in G$, define
$$f_g(x)=f(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)),\qquad [U_\mu(g)h](p)=e^{ip\circ a}h(\Lambda^{-1}p).$$
Then $f_g\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$, $U_\mu(g)$ is a well-defined unitary
on $H_\mu$, $g\mapsto U_\mu(g)$ is a strongly continuous representation, and
$$K_\mu f_g=U_\mu(g)K_\mu f \qquad(f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)).$$
The group product convention is
$(a,\Lambda)(b,\Gamma)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda\Gamma)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the scalar shell phase and test restriction, the invariant shell measure, and the proper orthochronous Minkowski action.

[A1] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The shell phase $p\circ x=-\eta(p,x)$ is Lorentz invariant and the test restriction is $\mathcal F_+f$ on the shell. [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]

[F2] The shell measure is locally finite, sigma-finite, and Lorentz invariant. [[lem-qft-mass-shell-measure-invariant]]

[F3] $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$ is contained in the shell restriction range in the massless chart and is dense there; the massive $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ chart functions are also in the range and dense. [[lem-qft-mass-shell-test-range-dense]]

[F4] $K_\mu$ maps every Schwartz test continuously into $H_\mu$. [[lem-qft-mass-shell-test-restriction-continuity]]

[F5] Proper orthochronous Lorentz maps preserve $\eta$, future orientation and orientation; in particular $|\det\Lambda|=1$. [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]

[F6] The chain rule applies to differentiable compositions. [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]

[F7] A $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open Euclidean sets satisfies change of variables for nonnegative measurable functions under Countable Choice. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]

[F8] Dominated convergence applies to an integrable majorant. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

## Proof

1.1 The affine pullback $f_g(x)=f(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ preserves Schwartz space. Repeated chain rule [F6] expresses each derivative as a finite linear combination of derivatives of $f$ at $\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)$. Also $1+|x|\le C(1+|\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)|)$ for a finite constant $C$ depending on $a,\Lambda$. Thus every polynomially weighted derivative remains bounded by the corresponding finite sum of Schwartz seminorms. [A1,F6,given,algebra]

1.2 Multiplication by $e^{ip\circ a}$ preserves the $H_\mu$ norm. Composition with $\Lambda^{-1}$ also preserves that norm by [F2]; it preserves null-equivalence classes for the same reason. Therefore $U_\mu(g)$ is a well-defined isometry. Its inverse is the corresponding formula for $g^{-1}$, so it is unitary. Direct substitution and Lorentz invariance of $p\circ x$ give $U_\mu(a,\Lambda)U_\mu(b,\Gamma) =U_\mu(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda\Gamma)$. [A1,F1,F2,F5,given,algebra]

2.1 In the Fourier integral for $K_\mu f_g$, change variables
$x=a+\Lambda y$; [F5] gives $|\det\Lambda|=1$ and [F7] justifies the
change of variables. The integrand is absolutely integrable because $f$ is
Schwartz; apply [F7] to the positive and negative parts of its real and
imaginary components to obtain this change of variables for the complex
integral. Lorentz invariance of the phase then gives
$$K_\mu f_g(p)=e^{ip\circ a}K_\mu f(\Lambda^{-1}p).$$
Both sides belong to $H_\mu$ by [F4], so this equality is also equality of
Hilbert-space vectors. This is the action formula used in step 1.2.
[A1,F1,F4,F5,F7,step 1.2,given,construct]

3.1 Let $h\in C_c^\infty$ in the shell chart, with support away from the
massless apex. If $g\to g_0$ in the Poincare group, $U_\mu(g)h$ converges
pointwise to $U_\mu(g_0)h$. In a compact neighborhood of $g_0$, the supports
lie in one compact chart subset $C$ away from the apex; $\nu_\mu(C)<\infty$
by [F2]. The squared pointwise difference is bounded by
$4\|h\|_\infty^2\mathbf1_C$, so [F8] gives norm continuity for this dense
family. Density follows from [F3]. For arbitrary $v\in H_\mu$, choose such
$h$ with $\|v-h\|<\epsilon$; unitarity gives
$$\|U_\mu(g)v-U_\mu(g_0)v\| \le2\epsilon+\|U_\mu(g)h-U_\mu(g_0)h\|.$$
First take $g\to g_0$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This proves strong
continuity on all of $H_\mu$. [A1,F2,F3,F8,step 1.2,given,algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a sigma-finite measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$;
a finite-valued measurable $\boldsymbol\omega:X\to\mathbb R^d$; and the
completed product measures and bosonic Fock construction.

[A1] Sigma-finite product measures exist, have the rectangle formula, and
their completions alter measurable sets only by null subsets.
[[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]
[[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]
[[def-completed-product-measure]] and uniqueness of the sigma-finite product
measure imply that finite products are independent of parenthesization and
invariant under coordinate permutations.
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[A2] Set $X^0=\{\star\}$ with sigma-algebra $\{\varnothing,\{\star\}\}$

$\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$ be the recursively defined product sigma-algebra and
let $\mu_n$ be the completion of the $n$-fold product measure on it. Thus in

[A3] Equip $\mathbb R^d$ with its Borel sigma-algebra

$E$ in the Statement is indexed by $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$, as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]].

[F1] The Fock space is the square-summable direct sum of its symmetric

[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]

[F2] For $n\ge2$, the product-tensor unitary sends
$f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n$ to $\prod_{r=1}^n f_r(x_r)$; iteration

[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]

[F3] Coordinate permutations act unitarily, and the symmetric sector is the

[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]

[F6] Dominated convergence and Fatou's lemma apply on each measure space

[[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F7] The complex exponential satisfies $|e^{itq}|=1$ for real $t,q$ and

## Proof

1.1 For $n\ge1$, each sector $H_s^{(n)}$ is a closed subspace of its Hilbert
tensor power, because it is the range of an orthogonal projection [F3]; the
zero-particle sector $H_s^{(0)}=\mathbb C$ is also complete. To prove that the
Fock direct sum is complete for arbitrary $H$, let $(\Psi^{(k)})_{k\ge1}$ be
Cauchy in its square-sum norm. Each coordinate is Cauchy in the complete
sector $H_s^{(n)}$, so it has a limit $\Psi_n$. A Cauchy sequence in a normed
space is bounded (its tail lies within distance $1$ of one fixed term, and
its finite initial segment is bounded); taking limits of each finite partial sum
$\sum_{n=0}^N\|\Psi_n^{(k)}\|^2$ shows
$\sup_N\sum_{n=0}^N\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty$, hence $\Psi=(\Psi_n)$ belongs to
the direct sum. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K$ so that
$\|\Psi^{(k)}-\Psi^{(\ell)}\|\le\varepsilon$ for $k,\ell\ge K$; for fixed
$k\ge K$, take $\ell\to\infty$ in every finite coordinate sum to obtain
$\sum_{n=0}^N\|\Psi_n^{(k)}-\Psi_n\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ for every $N$.
Taking the supremum over $N$ proves $\Psi^{(k)}\to\Psi$. Truncating the
coordinate sequence proves that $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense.
For $n=1$ use the identity in [F2]. For $n\ge2$, iterate the product-tensor
unitary of [F2]; induction gives a unitary from $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ to
the full completed-product $L^2(X^n,\mu_n)$. On elementary tensors the
permutation $U_\pi$ becomes coordinate permutation, so by density the
unitary intertwines $P_{s,n}$ with averaging over coordinate permutations
[F3]. Its restriction identifies $H_s^{(n)}$ with the closed symmetric
subspace. Each $s_n$ is Borel measurable by [A3], since it is a finite sum
of measurable coordinate maps, and is invariant under all permutations.
The $n=0$ sector is $\mathbb C$ by definition. [A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Let $\Omega=\bigsqcup_{n\ge0}X^n$ with the disjoint-union sigma-algebra and measure
$\mu_\Omega(C)=\sum_{n\ge0}\mu_n(C\cap X^n)$, using the conventions of [A2]; write $s_j$ for $s_{n,j}$ on component $n$. The Fock realization in step 1.1 is a closed subspace of $L^2(\Omega,\mu_\Omega)$ consisting of symmetric components. For $B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$, define $E(B)$ by multiplication by $\mathbf1_{s^{-1}(B)}$. Since $s$ is invariant under permutations, this multiplier preserves the symmetric subspace. It is an orthogonal projection because its multiplier is real and idempotent; $E(\varnothing)=0$, $E(\mathbb R^d)=I$ and $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$ follow pointwise. For pairwise disjoint $B_k\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ with union $B$, the squared norm of $E(B)\Psi-\sum_{k=0}^N E(B_k)\Psi$ is $$\sum_{n\ge0}\int_{X^n} \mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B\setminus\cup_{k=0}^N B_k)}|\Psi_n|^2\,d\mu_n.$$ The indicators tend pointwise to zero and the integrand is bounded by $|\Psi_n|^2$, whose total integral is $\|\Psi\|^2$; dominated convergence [F6] gives norm convergence. Hence $E$ is a strongly countably additive PVM on the Borel sets. [A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 Fix a real measurable multiplier $f$ on $\Omega$ that is invariant under coordinate permutations, and define $M_f\Psi=f\Psi$ on the symmetric domain $D(M_f)=\{\Psi:f\Psi\in L^2(\Omega)\}$. This domain is dense: the symmetric cutoffs $\Psi\mathbf1_{|f|\le m}$ belong to it and converge in norm by dominated convergence. Reality of $f$ makes $M_f$ symmetric. If $\Psi\in D(M_f^*)$ and $K=M_f^*\Psi$, then for each $m$ the vector $v_m=(f\Psi-K)\mathbf1_{|f|\le m}$ is symmetric and lies in $D(M_f)$, since $f$ is bounded on its support. The adjoint identity gives $$0=\langle M_fv_m,\Psi\rangle_2-\langle v_m,K\rangle_2 =\int_{|f|\le m}|f\Psi-K|^2\,d\mu_\Omega.$$ Taking the union over $m$ shows $f\Psi=K$ almost everywhere, so $\Psi\in D(M_f)$ and $M_f^*\Psi=M_f\Psi$. Conversely, for every $\Psi\in D(M_f)$, reality of $f$ gives the adjoint identity against every domain vector, so $M_f^*\Psi=M_f\Psi$. Therefore $M_f$ is self-adjoint on its maximal multiplication domain. Apply this to $f=s_j$ to obtain each self-adjoint $H_j$, and to $f=\theta\cdot s$ to obtain $H_\theta$. [F4, F6, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 For each $j$, the multiplier $s_j$ defines $H_j$ with the displayed component domain because the squared norm of $H_j\Psi$ is exactly $\sum_n\int|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2d\mu_n$; the vacuum term is zero. For $\theta$, the same calculation gives $D(H_\theta)=\{\Psi:\sum_n\int|\theta\cdot s_n|^2|\Psi_n|^2d\mu_n<\infty\}$. The PVM from step 2.1 has coordinate functions $s_j$, so its indicators give the joint spectral projections for all the $H_j$ and its scalar-coordinate multipliers have these exact domains. Truncating a vector in any such domain after sector $N$ makes both its norm tail and operator-image tail tend to zero; hence $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_\theta)$ are graph cores. [F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 By [F6], $U_\theta(t)$ is unitary and $U_\theta(t+s)=U_\theta(t)U_\theta(s)$ on each component, including the vacuum where the phase is one. For any $\Psi$, the squared norm of $U_\theta(t)\Psi-U_\theta(t_0)\Psi$ is the integral over $\Omega$ of $|e^{it\theta\cdot s}-e^{it_0\theta\cdot s}|^2|\Psi|^2$; the integrand tends pointwise to zero and is bounded by $4|\Psi|^2$, so [F6] proves strong continuity. If $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, the pointwise difference quotient tends to $i(\theta\cdot s)\Psi$ and its squared error is bounded by $4|\theta\cdot s|^2|\Psi|^2$; dominated convergence proves norm convergence. Conversely, if the difference quotient has a norm limit as $t\to0$, take $t_m=1/m$. Fatou's lemma [F6] on the disjoint union gives $$\sum_n\int|\theta\cdot s_n|^2|\Psi_n|^2d\mu_n \le\liminf_m\left\|\frac{U_\theta(t_m)\Psi-\Psi}{t_m}\right\|^2<\infty,$$ so $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$; the forward calculation identifies the limit as $iH_\theta\Psi$. This proves the exact derivative criterion and all claims. [F6, F7, step 3.1, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space, let $e\in H$ have norm one, and put
$K=e^\perp=\{v\in H:\langle e,v\rangle_2=0\}$. For
$\psi_m\in K_s^{(m)}$ and $k,m\ge0$, write
$|k\rangle:=e^{\otimes k}\in(\mathbb Ce)_s^{(k)}$ (with $|0\rangle=1$),
and define

$$J_{k,m}(|k\rangle\otimes\psi_m) =\sqrt{\binom{k+m}{k}}\, P_{s,k+m}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m).$$

The map $J_{k,m}$ extends over the sector Hilbert tensor products and the
orthogonal direct sums to a unitary

$$J:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb Ce)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(K) \longrightarrow\mathcal F_s(H).$$

Under this unitary, bosonic creation and annihilation by $e$ act on the first
factor as the one-mode ladder maps
$|k\rangle\mapsto\sqrt{k+1}|k+1\rangle$ and
$|k\rangle\mapsto\sqrt{k}|k-1\rangle$, respectively, tensored with the
identity on $\mathcal F_s(K)$, on finite-particle vectors.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a complex Hilbert space $H$ with a unit vector
$e$; the closed orthogonal complement $K=e^\perp$; bosonic Fock sectors and
creation/annihilation maps as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the Hilbert tensor constructions.
[[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Completed Hilbert tensor products have product inner products and dense
elementary tensors. [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]

[F2] $P_{s,n}$ is an orthogonal projection onto the symmetric sector; its
range is the set fixed by every permutation of tensor factors.
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]

[F3] The direct sum of square-summable sector sequences is the Fock space,
and creation on sector $n$ is $\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(e\otimes\cdot)$.
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]

[F4] The orthogonal complement $K=e^\perp$ is a closed linear subspace of
$H$, hence is a Hilbert space with its inherited inner product.
[[lem-orthogonal-complement-is-closed]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F4], $K$ is a Hilbert space, so its symmetric tensor sectors and
Fock space in the Statement are defined. Fix $k,m\ge0$, write $n=k+m$, and
let $\psi_m\in K_s^{(m)}$. Expanding
the permutation average and using symmetry of $\psi_m$ gives
$P_{s,n}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m)=\binom nk^{-1}\sum_{\substack{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\|I|=k}}v_I$, where $v_I$ is the tensor with $e$ in the slots in $I$ and the $m$ factors of
$\psi_m$ in the remaining slots, symmetrized there. Indeed, for each fixed
placement $I$, the $k!m!$ permutations of the equal $e$ factors and the
symmetric $\psi_m$ give the same tensor, and
$k!m!/n!=\binom nk^{-1}$. [A1, F2, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 Distinct placements $v_I$ are orthogonal: if $I\ne I'$, some slot contains $e$ in one tensor and a vector of $K$ in the other, and $e\perp K$. Each $v_I$ has norm $\|\psi_m\|$, so step 1.1 gives $\|P_{s,n}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m)\|^2 =\binom nk^{-1}\|\psi_m\|^2$. The same orthogonality shows that the images for different $k$ in a fixed $n$ sector are orthogonal. Thus the factor $\sqrt{\binom nk}$ makes $J_{k,m}$ isometric and their sector ranges are orthogonal. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 Algebraic elementary tensors in $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ are dense by [F1]. Expand each factor using $H=\mathbb Ce\oplus K$, distribute the finite tensor product, and apply $P_{s,n}$. Every resulting term has exactly $k$ factors $e$ and $m=n-k$ factors in $K$, so it lies in the range described in step 2.1. Since $P_{s,n}$ is bounded and algebraic elementary tensors are dense, their symmetrizations are dense in $H_s^{(n)}$; the range of the isometry is closed, hence it equals $H_s^{(n)}$. Taking the orthogonal direct sum over $n=k+m$ proves that $J$ is onto and unitary. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On a vector $e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m$ with $n=k+m$, creation by $e$ acts by $\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(e\otimes J_{k,m}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m))$. Since $P_{s,n+1}$ averages over all permutations, symmetrizing the last $n$ slots first does not change the result. This equals $\sqrt{n+1}\sqrt{\binom nk}P_{s,n+1}(e^{\otimes(k+1)}\otimes\psi_m)$. The binomial identity $\binom{n+1}{k+1}=\frac{n+1}{k+1}\binom nk$ makes this exactly $J_{k+1,m}(\sqrt{k+1}\,e^{\otimes(k+1)}\otimes\psi_m)$. Thus creation becomes the stated one-mode raising map. Annihilation by $e$ is zero for $k=0$, because every first tensor factor lies in $K$. For $k\ge1$, the placement formula of step 1.1 shows that contraction keeps exactly the $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ placements with $e$ in the contracted slot. Therefore $a(e)J_{k,m}\psi_m= \sqrt n\sqrt{\binom nk}\frac{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}{\binom nk} P_{s,n-1}(e^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\psi_m) =\sqrt k\,J_{k-1,m}\psi_m$, using $\binom nk=\frac nk\binom{n-1}{k-1}$. Thus annihilation becomes the stated one-mode lowering map and leaves the $K$ factor unchanged. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$H=L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ with its first-variable-linear integral pairing,
and let $Qf(x)=xf(x)$ on
$D(Q)=\{f\in H:xf\in H\}$. Let $(g_n)_{n\ge0}$ be the Hermite functions of
[[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]]. Then $Q$ is self-adjoint on $D(Q)$,
and the finite linear span of the $g_n$ is a core for $Q$: it is dense in
$D(Q)$ for the graph norm
$\|f\|_Q=(\|f\|_2^2+\|Qf\|_2^2)^{1/2}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb R)$; the
real multiplication map $Qf=xf$ on its maximal domain; and the Hermite
functions from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]].

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] $L^2(\mathbb R)$ is complete for its integral pairing and satisfies
Cauchy–Schwarz. [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]

[F2] The oscillator functions have the form
$g_n=H_ng_0/\sqrt{2^nn!}$, where $g_0(x)=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$, each $H_n$
has degree $n$ with nonzero leading coefficient, and
$\sqrt2\,xg_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$.
[[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]]

[F3] The $L^1$ Fourier transform uses
$\widehat h(\xi)=\int h(x)e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\,dx$; under Countable Choice it is
injective on $L^1(\mathbb R)$. [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]
[[cor-uniqueness-of-the-l-one-fourier-transform]]

[F4] The complex exponential is given by its everywhere convergent power
series, and dominated convergence applies to integrable majorants.
[[def-complex-exponential]]
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]
[[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F5] Polynomial multiples of a Gaussian and shifted Gaussian moments are
integrable. [[lem-euclidean-gaussian-fourier-transform-with-two-pi-normalization]]

[F6] In a Hilbert space, a subspace with zero orthogonal complement is dense.
[[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]
[[thm-double-orthogonal-complement-is-closure]]

## Proof

1.1 For $f\in H$, put $f_m=f\mathbf1_{[-m,m]}$. Then $f_m\in D(Q)$ because $|x|\le m$ on its support, and $f_m\to f$ in $L^2$ by dominated convergence applied to $|f_m-f|^2\le |f|^2$; hence $D(Q)$ is dense. For $f,g\in D(Q)$, $xf\overline g$ is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz, and real-valuedness of $x$ gives $\langle Qf,g\rangle=\langle f,Qg\rangle$. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

1.2 Equip $\mathcal G=\{f:\int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)|f(x)|^2dx<\infty\}$ with the explicit weighted inner product $\langle f,g\rangle_{\mathcal G}:=\int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$. Multiplication by $\sqrt{1+x^2}$ is an onto isometry from $\mathcal G$ to $L^2(\mathbb R)$, with inverse multiplication by $(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$, so $\mathcal G$ is Hilbert. Its norm equals $\|f\|_Q$ on $D(Q)$. Suppose $f\in\mathcal G$ is orthogonal to every $g_n$ in this weighted inner product. Since the $H_n$ have successive degrees and nonzero leading coefficients [F2], their finite span is all polynomials. Therefore $h(x)=(1+x^2)f(x)g_0(x)$ lies in $L^1$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and $\int h(x)x^jdx=0$ for every $j\ge0$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, construct]

2.1 Let $g\in D(Q^*)$ and write $k=Q^*g$. For each $m$, the vector $f_m=(xg-k)\mathbf1_{[-m,m]}$ belongs to $D(Q)$ since $x$ is bounded there and $g,k\in L^2$. The adjoint identity for $f_m$ yields $0=\langle Qf_m,g\rangle-\langle f_m,k\rangle =\int_{-m}^m|xg-k|^2\,dx$. Thus $xg=k$ almost everywhere on every $[-m,m]$, hence on $\mathbb R$; since $k\in L^2$, $g\in D(Q)$ and $Q^*g=Qg$. Conversely, symmetry in step 1.1 gives $D(Q)\subseteq D(Q^*)$ and $Q^*f=Qf$. Therefore $Q=Q^*$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

2.2 Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R$ and let $S_N(x)=\sum_{j=0}^N(-2\pi i\xi x)^j/j!$. By [F4], $S_N(x)\to e^{-2\pi i\xi x}$ and $|S_N(x)|\le e^{2\pi|\xi||x|}$. The majorant $|h(x)|e^{2\pi|\xi||x|}$ is integrable: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its integral by $\|f\|_{\mathcal G}\bigl(\int(1+x^2)g_0(x)^2e^{4\pi|\xi||x|}dx\bigr)^{1/2}$, and the latter integral is finite because completing the square gives $-x^2+4\pi|\xi||x|=-(|x|-2\pi|\xi|)^2+(2\pi|\xi|)^2$, so [F5] applies. Dominated convergence and the vanishing moments from step 1.2 imply $\widehat h(\xi)=\lim_N\int hS_N=0$. Since $\xi$ was arbitrary, $\widehat h$ vanishes identically. [step 1.2, F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

3.1 Fourier uniqueness [F3] gives $h=0$ almost everywhere. Since $1+x^2>0$ and $g_0(x)>0$ for every $x$, this implies $f=0$ in $\mathcal G$. Thus the orthogonal complement of the Hermite span in $\mathcal G$ is zero; [F6] makes that span dense in $\mathcal G$. Because the $\mathcal G$ norm is the graph norm of $Q$, the Hermite span is a graph core, proving the statement. [step 1.2, step 2.2, F2, F3, F6] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and let $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ be its bosonic Fock space and finite-particle domain.
For $h\in H$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the Segal field
$$\phi_0(h):=2^{-1/2}\bigl(a^\dagger(h)+a(h)\bigr).$$
For $h\ne0$, this symmetric operator is essentially self-adjoint; write
$\Phi(h)=\overline{\phi_0(h)}$. If $r=\|h\|$, $e=h/r$, $K=e^\perp$,
$G=\mathcal F_s(K)$, choose a countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $G$
whose vectors are finite-particle, and use the one-mode splitting of
[[lem-qft-fock-one-mode-splitting]] followed by the Hermite unitary
$|n\rangle\mapsto g_n$ into $L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ with pairing
$\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int\overline f g$ to write a vector as
$(f_j)_{j\in J}\in\ell^2(J;L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C))$. Then the exact domain and
action are
$$D(\Phi(h))=\left\{(f_j):\sum_{j\in J}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+r^2x^2)|f_j(x)|^2\,dx<\infty\right\},\qquad (\Phi(h)f)_j(x)=rx f_j(x).$$
For $h=0$, $\phi_0(0)$ closes to the zero operator on all of $\mathcal F_s(H)$.

Define $\epsilon(z)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}z^{\otimes n}/\sqrt{n!}$ for $z\in H$.
There are unitaries $W(h)$ determined on these total exponential vectors by
$$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$
They obey
$$W(h)W(k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{2}\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle_2\right)W(h+k),\qquad \langle\Omega,W(h)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|h\|^2/4},$$
and $h\mapsto W(h)$ is strongly continuous. For every $h$, the one-parameter
group $t\mapsto W(th)$ has norm derivative at zero exactly on
$D(\Phi(h))$, with derivative $i\Phi(h)$ (for $h=0$ this is the zero
generator). Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the
closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim
is included.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a separable complex Hilbert space $H$; its
bosonic Fock sectors, vacuum, finite-particle domain and creation/annihilation
maps; and the Hermite functions $g_n$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the choice assumption of the Fock tensor and sector
constructions. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] On finite sectors, $a(h)$ is conjugate-linear in $h$, $a^\dagger(h)$ is
linear, and they are mutual adjoints between adjacent sectors; their sector
norms are at most $\sqrt n\|h\|$ and $\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|$.
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]

[F2] For a unit vector $e$, $H=\mathbb Ce\oplus e^\perp$ and the map
$J(|k\rangle\otimes\psi_m)=\sqrt{\binom{k+m}{k}}
P_{s,k+m}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m)$ extends to a unitary from
$\mathcal F_s(\mathbb Ce)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(e^\perp)$ to
$\mathcal F_s(H)$; $a(e)$ and $a^\dagger(e)$ become the one-mode lowering and
raising maps. [[lem-qft-fock-one-mode-splitting]]

[F3] The real Hermite functions $g_n=H_ng_0/\sqrt{2^nn!}$ form an
orthonormal basis of Lebesgue $L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$, with $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=2x$,
$H_{n+1}=2xH_n-2nH_{n-1}$, and
$xg_n=(\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1})/\sqrt2$.
[[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]
[[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]]

[F4] Multiplication $Qf(x)=xf(x)$ is self-adjoint, and the finite Hermite
span is a core in its graph norm. The graph, adjoint, and core terms have the
definitions in [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]],
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], and
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]]. The cited core result
uses first-variable-linear $L^2$; complex conjugation transfers it to the
second-variable-linear pairing used here, because $Q$ and every $g_n$ are
real. [[lem-qft-hermite-graph-core-for-position]]

[F5] For a densely defined operator $T$, $y\in D(T^*)$ exactly when there is
$w$ with $\langle Tx,y\rangle_2=\langle x,w\rangle_2$ for all $x\in D(T)$;
the real multiplication operator is symmetric when its multiplier is real.
This is the adjoint convention of
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]] after reversing the
pairing, together with [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]].

These vectors are total: if $\Psi=(\Psi_n)$ is orthogonal to all of them, then for every $z$ and scalar $t$ the entire power series $\langle\Psi,\epsilon(tz)\rangle_2$ vanishes, so each coefficient $\langle\Psi_n,z^{\otimes n}\rangle_2$ is zero. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let

$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

$$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4):=\{F=(F_0,F_1,F_2,F_3):F_a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)\text{ for }a=0,1,2,3\},$$

$$\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}F(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad u_F(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)\,dt.$$
Then $u_F\in\mathcal H_D$, continuously in the Schwartz topology, and
$$\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})$$
defines a bounded operator on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-})$, antilinear in $F$. It satisfies
$$\{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)\}=0,\qquad \{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)^\dagger\}=\langle u_F,u_G\rangle_{\mathcal H_D}I.$$
The positive and negative contraction kernels, defined as tempered distributions by their Fourier integrals, are
$$C_+(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{-i(\omega\tau-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_+(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3},\qquad C_-(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{+i(\omega\tau+\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_-(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}.$$
Their tested pairings give respectively $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$; their sum is the anticommutator kernel $R$ below.
Its tested free equation is $u_{(i\partial_0-h_D(-i\nabla))F}=0$. For spatial Schwartz spinors $u,v$, the equal-time field $\Psi_t(u)=c(P_+W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u})$ satisfies $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)^\dagger\}=\int u(\mathbf x)^\dagger v(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x\,I$ and $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)\}=0$.

The spacetime anticommutator kernel is
$$R(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}W_D(-\tau,\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}=\partial_\tau\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x)I_4-i h_D(-i\nabla)\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x),$$

Spinor tests with compact spacelike-separated supports have vanishing anticommutators with one another and with each other's adjoints. Consequently, even polynomials in the bounded smeared fields commute across spacelike-separated regions. These are mathematical properties of the specified free-field construction.

The integral is finite because $0\le b_d\le1$ and its support lies in a
