## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the bounded linear operators on $H$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); for $M\in\mathcal B(H)$, $M^*$ is its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

Under this same $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis, [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]] gives $M^*\in\mathcal B(H)$ and $\|M^*\|=\|M\|$.

A **finite bounded Kraus instrument datum** on $H$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, integers $q_a\ge0$ for $a=1,\ldots,m$, and bounded operators $M_{a,r}\in\mathcal B(H)$ for $r=1,\ldots,q_a$. It is **normalized** when

$$\sum_{a=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H.$$

Empty inner sums are zero. For each outcome $a$, define its outcome operator and operation by

$$E_a:=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad \mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*\quad(X\in\mathcal B(H)).$$

These formulas take values in $\mathcal B(H)$: the adjoint theorem above makes each $M_{a,r}^*$ bounded, and $\|M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*x\|\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|X\|\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\,\|x\|=\|M_{a,r}\|^2\,\|X\|\,\|x\|$; the sums are finite. This definition specifies only the displayed finite Kraus form; it is not a representation theorem for arbitrary instruments and does not assert that an apparatus realizes these data.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ carry a normalized finite bounded Kraus instrument datum as defined in [[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]], and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $H$: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]], [[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). For each outcome $a$, put $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho))$. Then each $E_a$ is an effect ($E_a\ge0$ and $I_H-E_a\ge0$), each $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is positive trace class, and

$$p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\in[0,1],\qquad \sum_{a=1}^{m}p_a=1.$$

The nonselective output $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is a density operator. If $p_a>0$, the normalized conditional state $\rho_a:=\mathcal J_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator; when $p_a=0$, this normalized update is undefined. For a unit vector $\psi\in H$, the rank-one density operator $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ has outcome probability $p_a=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$. These are conditional mathematical identities; they do not assert that an apparatus realizes the instrument or supply a physical measurement postulate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a nonzero complex Hilbert space $H$; a normalized finite bounded Kraus instrument datum $(M_{a,r})$; and a density operator $\rho$ on $H$.

[A1] Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) is assumed for the adjoint and trace-class definitions and suppliers, and for the density expansion [F1]. No stronger choice principle is invoked.

[L1] [[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]]: the outcome operators are $E_a=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$, the maps are $\mathcal J_a(X)=\sum_rM_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*$, and normalization means $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H$. The adjoint obeys $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$.

[F1] [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]: under Countable Choice, a density operator is self-adjoint, positive and trace class with trace one, and has a trace-norm convergent expansion $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ with $(u_j)$ orthonormal, $w_j\ge0$ and $\sum_jw_j=1$. We use statement (a); its separate statement (c) is not used.

[F2] [[lem-nrqm-composites-nuclear-bounded-cyclicity]]: under Countable Choice, bounded multiplication of a nuclear representation gives trace-norm-convergent series for $BT$ and $TB$, with $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle$, $\operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle$, absolute convergence, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$. No unbounded factor is cyclically permuted.

[F3] [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]: $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ is trace class with $\|T_{u,v}\|_1=\|u\|\,\|v\|$ and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$; $T_{x,x}$ is self-adjoint and positive.

[F4] [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]: for bounded $B$, $BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v}$ and $T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v}$.

[F5] [[def-trace-class-operator]]: a trace-class operator is in $\mathcal B(H)$ and has finite trace norm. [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]] defines the trace relative to a supplied Hilbert basis. [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]] proves basis independence, linearity and $|\operatorname{tr}T|\le\|T\|_1$, hence continuity in trace norm.

[F6] [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]: positivity means that the quadratic-form values $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ are real and nonnegative; self-adjointness is the separate identity $T^*=T$.

[F7] [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]: under Countable Choice, if $T$ is trace class and $A,B$ are bounded, then $ATB$ is trace class and $\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\|$.

[F8] [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the Hilbert adjoint of every bounded operator $M$ is bounded, $\|M^*\|=\|M\|$, and $M^{**}=M$.

## Proof

1.1 For each $a,r$, $M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ is bounded by [F8]. Also [F8] gives $M_{a,r}^{**}=M_{a,r}$, so $\langle M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}x,y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}x,M_{a,r}^{**}y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}x,M_{a,r}y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}y\rangle$; hence it is self-adjoint. Its quadratic form is $\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\ge0$. Hence $E_a\ge0$. Normalization gives $I_H-E_a=\sum_{b\ne a}\sum_rM_{b,r}^*M_{b,r}\ge0$, including empty sums, so $E_a$ is an effect. [given, L1, F6, F8, algebra]

1.2 By [F8], each $M_{a,r}^*$ is bounded, so [F7] makes $M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*$ trace class; the finite sum $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is trace class. By [F8], $M_{a,r}^{**}=M_{a,r}$, and for all $x,y\in H$,
$\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,y\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}^*x,\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^{**}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle$,
where the first equality uses the adjoint identity for $M_{a,r}$, the second uses $\rho=\rho^*$, and the fourth uses the adjoint identity for $M_{a,r}^*$. Also $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,x\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*x\rangle\ge0$. Finite summation shows $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is self-adjoint and positive. [given, A1, L1, F1, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], write $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ in trace norm. For its partial sums $\rho_N=\sum_{j\le N}w_jT_{u_j,u_j}$, [F8] gives $\|M_{a,r}^*\|=\|M_{a,r}\|<\infty$, so [F7] gives $\|M_{a,r}(\rho-\rho_N)M_{a,r}^*\|_1\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|\rho-\rho_N\|_1\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\to0$. Thus [F4] gives $\mathcal J_a(\rho)=\sum_{r,j}w_jT_{M_{a,r}u_j,M_{a,r}u_j}$ in trace norm; the trace-norm sum is finite since $\sum_jw_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\le\|M_{a,r}\|^2\sum_jw_j=\|M_{a,r}\|^2$ for each $r$. Trace continuity [F5] and [F3] yield $p_a=\sum_{r,j}w_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\ge0$. Cyclicity [F2] gives $p_a=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$. [given, A1, L1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Because the outcome and Kraus index sets are finite, [F1] and step 2.1 give $\sum_ap_a=\sum_jw_j\langle(\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jw_j\|u_j\|^2=1$ by normalization. Since every $p_a\ge0$, this also gives $p_a\le1$ for every $a$. [given, A1, L1, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $p_a>0$, step 1.2 gives a positive trace-class numerator $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ and step 2.1 gives its trace $p_a$, so $\rho_a=\mathcal J_a(\rho)/p_a$ is positive trace class with trace one, hence a density operator by [F1]. The finite sum $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is likewise positive trace class, and its trace is $\sum_ap_a=1$ by step 3.1, so it is a density operator. If $p_a=0$, division by $p_a$ is undefined and no normalized update is asserted. [given, A1, L1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F5, algebra]

5.1 For a unit vector $\psi$, [F3] gives that $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class with trace $\|\psi\|^2=1$, hence a density operator by [F1]. Also [F4] gives $M_{a,r}T_{\psi,\psi}M_{a,r}^*=T_{M_{a,r}\psi,M_{a,r}\psi}$. Taking traces and summing over the finite Kraus list yields $p_a=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$, as claimed. [given, L1, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix $\mu\ge0$, $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$, and the Dirac matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]; $\mu$ is the inverse-length mathematical shell parameter of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. For a smooth real scalar field $\phi$ and smooth commuting complex spinor $\psi:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$, use the normalized free Lagrangian densities
$$\mathcal L_\phi=-\frac12\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b\phi+\mu^2\phi^2\right),\qquad \mathcal L_D=\bar\psi\left(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu\right)\psi,\qquad \bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta.$$
For compactly supported smooth real variations $h$ and compactly supported smooth complex spinor variations $\chi$, the action symbols are used only through the following finite, compactly supported first variations; no global integrability of the background fields is assumed:
$$\delta S_\phi(\phi;h)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h(\Box-\mu^2)\phi\,d^4x,\qquad \delta S_D(\psi;\chi)=2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R^4}\chi^\dagger\beta\left(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu\right)\psi\,d^4x.$$
Each field is stationary under all such variations if and only if its corresponding Euler–Lagrange equation holds pointwise:
$$(\Box-\mu^2)\phi=0,\qquad (i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0.$$
The adjoint Dirac equation follows from the second equation because the fixed matrices satisfy $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$. These are mathematical variation identities for commuting classical fields; they assert no quantization, Grassmann calculus, or physical measurement.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mu\ge0$, the fixed metric and shell conventions, the Dirac matrix representation, and the stated spaces of compactly supported smooth variations.

[A1] The parameter $\mu$ is a nonnegative inverse-length shell parameter and $\Box=-\partial_0^2+\Delta_{\mathbf x}$. [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]

[F1] The Pauli matrices $\sigma_j$ are Hermitian. The fixed Dirac block representation is
$$\beta=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2),\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j,\qquad \bar z=z^\dagger\beta.$$
[[def-qft-dirac-projections]]

[F2] A variation belongs to $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)$; real scalar variations are its real-valued members. [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]

[F3] Every open ball contains a nonnegative smooth compactly supported bump that is positive on a smaller concentric ball. [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]

[F4] The iterated integrals of the compactly supported smooth products below agree by Fubini's theorem. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F4].

1.1 For the scalar action, differentiating its density at $\phi+\varepsilon h$ gives
$$\delta S_\phi=-\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b h+\mu^2\phi h\right)d^4x.$$
For each coordinate, the product $\partial_a\phi\,h$ has compact support; one-dimensional integration by parts on that coordinate has zero boundary term, and Fubini [F4] permits integrating the remaining coordinates. Hence
$$\delta S_\phi=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\phi-\mu^2\phi\right)d^4x=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h(\Box-\mu^2)\phi\,d^4x.$$

[F1] [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]]: the Fourier characters $e_{\mathbf n}$ form a basis of $L^2(\mathbb T^E)$, the finite CAR occupation vectors form an orthonormal basis, and $G_x$ acts diagonally by $\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)$. The QFT-MF01 Fock definition and CAR lemma are current batch-37 draft carriers; their statements and proof interfaces were inspected, and this use remains conditional because they have no Step-1 readiness records.

## Proof

**Given:** The data and conventions in [F1].

1.1 The finite-support linear combinations of the joint basis vectors are dense in $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$. On each joint basis vector, $G_x$ multiplies by the real number $\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)$. The maximal diagonal operator is self-adjoint: if $\phi\in D(G_x^*)$ and $G_x^*\phi=\eta$, testing the adjoint identity against each basis vector gives $\eta_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}=\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)\phi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}$. Since $\eta\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$, the defining weighted square sum for $D(G_x)$ is finite, so $D(G_x^*)\subseteq D(G_x)$; conversely Cauchy–Schwarz gives the adjoint identity for every $\phi\in D(G_x)$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Every $G_x$ is diagonal in the same basis. Thus the spectral projections of any two $G_x$ are diagonal coordinate projections and commute, which proves strong commutation. On a basis vector, $U(\alpha)$ multiplies by $e^{i\sum_x\alpha_x\gamma_x}$; integer $\gamma_x$ makes it $2\pi$-periodic in each coordinate, and the diagonal phases give $U(\alpha+\beta)=U(\alpha)U(\beta)$ and $U(0)=I$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For finite linear combinations of basis vectors, $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$ is a finite sum of continuous characters. Such vectors are dense and all $U(\alpha)$ have norm one, so for arbitrary $\psi$ approximation by a finite combination proves norm continuity of $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$. This is strong continuity. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 From $[E_e,U_f]=\delta_{ef}U_f$ and $[n_y,c_{x\beta}]=-\delta_{xy}c_{x\beta}$ on the finite occupation core, one has $[G_x,U_e]=(\mathbf1_{x=s(e)}-\mathbf1_{x=t(e)})U_e$ and $[G_x,c_{y\beta}]=\delta_{xy}c_{y\beta}$. Exponentiating these exact shifts on the joint basis yields the two displayed gauge-transformation laws. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For every $\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$, strong continuity from step 3.1 makes $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$ continuous on the compact torus. Its Hilbert-valued Riemann sums converge in norm: uniform continuity makes sums over partitions of mesh tending to zero a Cauchy family, and completeness supplies their limit. The normalized integral therefore exists, and its operator norm is at most one because each summand is an average of unitary images. For a basis vector with charge labels $\gamma=(\gamma_x)$, that integral is the vector itself if $\gamma=0$ and zero otherwise, since $(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{ik\alpha}\,d\alpha=\mathbf1_{k=0}$ for each integer $k$. By density of finite-support vectors and the norm bound, $P$ is the diagonal multiplier $\mathbf1_{\gamma=0}$ on all of $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$; hence $P=P^*=P^2$ and its range is exactly the joint kernel of the $G_x$. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For each $x$, choose any $b_x$ of the $s$ fermion modes at that site to occupy. The occupation vector so obtained is normalized and has $n_x=b_x$; tensoring it with the zero-link Fourier basis vector gives every $\gamma_x=0$. Thus it is a nonzero vector in $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. [F1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the data of [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]] and let $R\subseteq V$. Define
$$\partial R=\{e\in E:\text{exactly one endpoint of }e\text{ lies in }R\},$$
with $\epsilon(e,R)=1$ when $s(e)\in R,t(e)\notin R$ and $\epsilon(e,R)=-1$ when $t(e)\in R,s(e)\notin R$. On the domain
$$\mathcal D_R=\mathcal H_{\rm phys}\cap\bigcap_{e\in\partial R}D(E_e),$$
the region number $N_R=\sum_{x\in R}(n_x-b_xI)$ obeys the exact identity
$$N_R\psi=\left(\sum_{e\in\partial R}\epsilon(e,R)E_e\right)\psi\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal D_R).$$
Thus for $R=V$, where $\partial R=\varnothing$, every physical vector has total occupation $\sum_x n_x=\sum_x b_x$. This finite-graph identity is exact and makes no continuum-limit claim.



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite oriented graph, the joint diagonal Gauss operators, and their physical joint kernel.

[F1] [[lem-qft-lattice-gauss-projection]]: in the Fourier/occupation basis $G_x$ multiplies by $\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)=\sum_{s(e)=x}n_e-\sum_{t(e)=x}n_e-(m_x-b_x)$, and $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\bigcap_x\ker G_x$.

## Proof

**Given:** [F1] and $R\subseteq V$.

1.1 For every basis label $(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)$, summing $\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)$ over $x\in R$ cancels each link with both endpoints in $R$, leaves $+\!n_e$ on a link directed out of $R$ and $-\!n_e$ on a link directed into $R$, and subtracts $\sum_{x\in R}(m_x-b_x)$. Therefore $$\sum_{x\in R}\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)=\sum_{e\in\partial R}\epsilon(e,R)n_e-\sum_{x\in R}(m_x-b_x).$$ [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The equality of basis multipliers in step 1.1 is an equality of diagonal operators on vectors for which both sides are defined. Every $\psi\in\mathcal D_R$ is in all $D(G_x)$ by physicality and in each boundary $D(E_e)$ by definition, while $N_R$ is bounded; applying the multiplier identity gives $\sum_{x\in R}G_x\psi=(\sum_{e\in\partial R}\epsilon(e,R)E_e-N_R)\psi$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\psi\in\mathcal D_R\subseteq\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, then $G_x\psi=0$ for every $x\in R$. Substitution in step 2.1 gives the claimed regional charge/flux identity. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 For $R=V$, every link has both endpoints in $R$, so $\partial R=\varnothing$ and the flux sum is zero. Step 3.1 then yields $N_V\psi=0$, which is exactly $\sum_x n_x\psi=(\sum_x b_x)\psi$ on all of $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Construction

Use two vertices $v_1,v_2$, one link $e:v_1\to v_2$, one fermion mode per vertex, and $b_{v_1}=b_{v_2}=0$. A state with exactly one occupied fermion mode cannot be physical, whatever link-electric basis label is chosen: summing the two Gauss equations fixes total occupation to zero.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and the $L^2$ Hilbert-space and Fock-pairing conventions stated above.

[A1] Under Countable Choice, complex $L^2(\mu)$ with the integral pairing is a Hilbert space. [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]

[A2] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The Fock convention uses a second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing. [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]

[F2] The Euclidean dot product is $u\cdot v=\sum_{i=1}^3u_iv_i$ and $|u|=\sqrt{u\cdot u}$. [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1], [F2], and the measurable matrix field in the definition.

1.1 For each $\mathbf k\ne0$, $n^Tn=n\cdot n=1$ by [F2], so $P_T^*=P_T$ and
$$P_T^2=(I-nn^T)^2=I-2nn^T+n(n^Tn)n^T=I-nn^T=P_T.$$
Its complex kernel is $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{n\}$ and its
range is the Hermitian perpendicular plane $n^\perp$, of complex dimension
two. For $z\in\mathbb C^3$, put $a=n^Tz$. The specified Hermitian pairing
and realness of $n$ give
$\|P_Tz\|^2=\sum_j|z_j-n_ja|^2=\|z\|^2-|a|^2\le\|z\|^2$.
Thus it is contractive, with norm one because it fixes every unit vector in
that nonzero perpendicular plane. The arbitrary value at the single point $\mathbf k=0$ does not affect its multiplication operator on $L^2$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Under [A2], [A1] makes each complex scalar $L^2$ component complete for its first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=\int u\overline v$. The three-component direct sum is complete componentwise. Its second-variable-linear pairing is $\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1=\int\overline u\cdot v$, with the same norm; [F1] fixes this convention. Thus $\mathcal H$ is complete. The multiplier $M_{P_T}$ is bounded and idempotent by step 1.1. If $u_r=M_{P_T}v_r\to u$ in $\mathcal H$, then $M_{P_T}u=\lim_rM_{P_T}u_r=\lim_ru_r=u$ by boundedness, so $u$ belongs to its range. Thus $\mathcal H_T$ is closed and inherits a positive Hilbert inner product. Since $P_Tu=u$ is equivalent to $n\cdot u=0$ for unit $n$ by [F2], the pointwise range formula gives the displayed transverse condition almost everywhere. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $j=(j_1,j_2,j_3)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ and use $\mathcal H_T$ and $P_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. For $\omega=|\mathbf k|$ and $\mathbf k\ne0$, define
$$g_j(\mathbf k)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}}\, P_T(\mathbf k)\int_{\mathbb R^4}j(x)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^4x.$$
Then $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$. On the finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$, the smeared transverse potential is
$$A_T(j)=a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j).$$
Its matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology; it is an operator-valued distribution and does not assign a pointwise operator to $A_i(x)$. With $E_i=-\partial_0A_i$, the equal-time canonical commutator is the distribution
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)] =-i\,P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; compact smooth real vector tests; the transverse projection; and the bosonic Fock CCR on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

[A1] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] $P_T$ is an orthogonal projection of norm at most one and $\mathcal H_T$ is its closed range. [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]

[F2] On finite-particle vectors, $[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I$ and the sector maps have bounds $\|a_n(h)\|\le\sqrt n\|h\|$, $\|a_n^\dagger(h)\|\le\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|$. [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]

[F3] Bosonic Fock space is the square-summable direct sum of symmetric particle sectors, $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of vectors with only finitely many nonzero sectors, and the test class $C_c^\infty$ has its locally convex LF topology. [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]

[F4] Assuming Countable Choice, finite rational linear combinations of indicators of rational boxes form a countable dense subset of real $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$. [[thm-rational-box-step-functions-form-a-countable-dense-subset-of-l-p-of-rn]]

[F5] A finite product of at most countable sets is at most countable, by iterating the two-set product theorem. [[thm-product-of-countable]]

[F6] A topological space is separable when it has an at most countable dense subset. [[def-separable-space]]

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3], and the test $j$ in the statement.

1.1 The integral in $g_j$ is the spacetime Fourier transform of a compactly supported smooth function, hence decreases faster than every inverse power of $|(\omega,\mathbf k)|$ by repeated integration by parts. Near $\mathbf k=0$, it is bounded by $\int|j|$, while the squared prefactor is $1/(2\omega)=1/(2|\mathbf k|)$. The radial integral of this bound is a constant times $\int_0^1r^2/r\,dr<\infty$. At infinity the rapid Fourier decay and $\|P_T\|\le1$ make the squared norm integrable. Also $P_Tg_j=g_j$ almost everywhere. Therefore $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 To apply [F2] with one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$, first verify its separability hypothesis. Let $D$ be the countable dense subset of real $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ supplied by [F4]. Its sixfold product is countable by [F5]; identifying each tuple with a three-component complex function whose real and imaginary components lie in $D$ gives a dense subset of $\mathcal H$. Density follows by approximating the six real $L^2$ components, since the squared complex-vector norm is the sum of their squared norms. Hence $\mathcal H$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6]. The image of this countable set under the bounded projection $M_{P_T}$ is countable and dense in $\mathcal H_T$: for $u\in\mathcal H_T$, $M_{P_T}u=u$, so projected approximants to $u$ converge to $u$. Thus $\mathcal H_T$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6], and [F2] applies. By [F3], a vector in $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has only finitely many nonzero sectors. On each such sector [F2] bounds creation and annihilation by the corresponding square-root particle number times $\|g_j\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Thus both maps and their sum are defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The same estimates bound every matrix element between fixed finite-particle vectors by a constant times $\|g_j\|$. On each fixed compact support, repeated integration by parts in step 1.1 bounds $\|g_j\|$ by finitely many smooth-test seminorms, so these matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology. This proves the asserted distributional smearing without defining a point field. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Write $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, and use the Fourier convention $\widehat f(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(\mathbf x)e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^3\mathbf x$. The expansion implied by the definition of $g_j$ is
$$A_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}}\left(a_i(\mathbf k)e^{-i\omega x^0+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}+a_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\right),$$
$$E_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=-\partial_0A_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(ia_i(\mathbf k)e^{-i\omega x^0+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}-ia_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\right).$$
Smearing the first line with $j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ gives exactly $a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j)$: the annihilation term uses conjugate-linearity of $a$, while the creation term is linear in its argument.
Here the formula is for $\mathbf k\ne0$; values at $\mathbf k=0$ are irrelevant to the integrals. The symbols $a_i(\mathbf k)$ and $a_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)$ are distributional notation for the Fock maps: for Schwartz vectors $u,v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^3$ set $a(u):=a(P_Tu)$ and $a^\dagger(v):=a^\dagger(P_Tv)$. Then [F2] gives $[a(u),a^\dagger(v)]=\int\overline{u_i(\mathbf k)}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)v_j(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k\,I$, equivalently the kernel notation $[a_i(\mathbf k),a_j^\dagger(\mathbf q)]=P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\delta^3(\mathbf k-\mathbf q)I$. The mode integrals are understood after test smearing; near $\mathbf k=0$ their squared one-particle weights behave respectively as $1/\omega$ and $\omega$, both locally integrable against $d^3\mathbf k$, and at infinity the Fourier transforms of the spatial tests decrease rapidly. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 For real $f,h\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, define the equal-time spatial smearings by pairing the mode distributions with the spatial tests, $A(f):=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^3}f_i(\mathbf x)A_i(0,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x$ and $E(h):=\sum_j\int_{\mathbb R^3}h_j(\mathbf y)E_j(0,\mathbf y)\,d^3\mathbf y$. The one-particle vectors in these definitions are
$$g_f(\mathbf k)=\frac{P_T(\mathbf k)\widehat f(\mathbf k)}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}},\qquad e_h(\mathbf k)=-i\frac{\omega^{1/2}P_T(\mathbf k)\widehat h(\mathbf k)}{(2\pi)^{3/2}2^{1/2}}.$$
These belong to $\mathcal H_T$ by the preceding bounds, and $A(f)=a(g_f)+a^\dagger(g_f)$, $E(h)=a(e_h)+a^\dagger(e_h)$. The CCR [F2] gives
$$[A(f),E(h)]=-i\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}\,\overline{\widehat f_i(\mathbf k)}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\widehat h_j(\mathbf k)\,I.$$
For real $f,h$, this Fourier integral is real because $P_T$ is real and even and $\widehat f(-\mathbf k)=\overline{\widehat f(\mathbf k)}$, $\widehat h(-\mathbf k)=\overline{\widehat h(\mathbf k)}$.
Equivalently, as a tempered distribution in $\mathbf z=\mathbf x-\mathbf y$,
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)]=-iK_{ij}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y),\qquad K_{ij}(\mathbf z)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf z}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
The last integral defines a tempered distribution because $P_T$ is measurable and bounded: for $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$ its pairing is $(2\pi)^{-3}\int P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\widehat\varphi(-\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k$, which is absolutely convergent. Since the Fourier symbol of $P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla)$ is $P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)$, this distribution is exactly $P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)$. The sign is negative because $E=-\partial_0A$: the annihilation/creation cross terms contribute $-i/2$ each at equal time. Thus the stated equal-time commutator holds distributionally after smearing, with its stated sign. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $G(\mathbf x)=1/(4\pi|\mathbf x|)$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, interpreted as its locally integrable distribution, and use the Fourier convention
$$\widehat f(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}f(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad f(\mathbf x)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\widehat f(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
Then $\mathcal F^{-1}(|\mathbf k|^{-2})=G$ distributionally. Consequently, for $P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)=\delta_{ij}-k_i k_j/|\mathbf k|^2$,
$$P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla)\delta^3 =\delta_{ij}\delta^3+\partial_i\partial_jG.$$
For $\mathbf x\ne0$,
$$\partial_i\partial_jG(\mathbf x) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{4\pi|\mathbf x|^3} +\frac{3x_ix_j}{4\pi|\mathbf x|^5}.$$
Thus the equal-time transverse-potential commutator of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]] has this off-diagonal Newtonian kernel (with its stated factor $-i$). The identity is distributional at the origin; the displayed classical derivative formula is only asserted away from it.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F8] and the Fourier convention in the statement.

1.1 For $\varepsilon>0$, $m_\varepsilon(\mathbf k)=e^{-\varepsilon|\mathbf k|}/|\mathbf k|^2$ is integrable: [F3] and $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ give $\int|m_\varepsilon|d^3\mathbf k=4\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon s}ds<\infty$. Its inverse Fourier integral is radial. Rotate the polar axis to $\mathbf x$ using [F4], and apply the zonal identity separately to the real and imaginary parts of $u\mapsto e^{is|\mathbf x|u}$. The polar formula [F3] is stated for nonnegative Borel functions; since this complex integrand is absolutely integrable, apply it separately to the positive and negative parts of its real and imaginary parts and recombine by [F5]. The angular integral is $4\pi\sin(s r)/(s r)$, where $r=|\mathbf x|$. Thus
$$G_\varepsilon(r)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}m_\varepsilon(\mathbf k)d^3\mathbf k =\frac1{2\pi^2r}\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon s}\frac{\sin(sr)}s\,ds.$$
Since $\sin(sr)/s=\int_0^r\cos(st)dt$ and $\int_0^r\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon s}|\cos(st)|dsdt\le r/\varepsilon$, Fubini [F7] applies. The real part of $\int_0^\infty e^{-(\varepsilon-it)s}ds=(\varepsilon-it)^{-1}$ is $\varepsilon/(\varepsilon^2+t^2)$; integrating it over $t\in[0,r]$ gives $\arctan(r/\varepsilon)$. Therefore
$$G_\varepsilon(r)=\frac{\arctan(r/\varepsilon)}{2\pi^2r}.$$
[A1, F3, F4, F5, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 For every test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ [F8], the bound $|G_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)|\le(4\pi|\mathbf x|)^{-1}$ and [F3] make $G_\varepsilon\varphi$ dominated by an integrable function; [F5] gives the distributional limit $G_\varepsilon\to G$. To identify the same limit in Fourier variables, repeated integration by parts in a coordinate with $|k_j|\ge|\mathbf k|/\sqrt3$ gives $|\widehat\varphi(\mathbf k)|\le C_N(1+|\mathbf k|)^{-N}$ for every integer $N$, while $|\widehat\varphi|\le\|\varphi\|_1$ near zero. Use the fixed Minkowski coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)=(ct,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, on an open coordinate domain $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with its standard topology. Each $x^a$ has unit metre. For a smooth scalar component $u:U\to\mathbb R$ or $u:U\to\mathbb C$, define $\partial_a u:=\partial u/\partial x^a$; thus $\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t$ at fixed $\mathbf x$, $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x^j$ for $j=1,2,3$, and each $\partial_a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Raise derivative indices with $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$. The fields in this definition are smooth maps
$$\phi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathbf A\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R^3),\qquad \psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4),\qquad \chi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R).$$
Define the lower-potential component maps $A_a:U\to\mathbb R$ by $A_0=-\phi/c$ and $A_j=\mathbf A_j$; collectively $(A_a)$ is the real covector potential in this chart. Then $F_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ has smooth real component maps $F_{ab}:U\to\mathbb R$. The spinor is an ordinary commuting $\mathbb C^4$-valued map, not a tuple of Grassmann generators. Its Dirac adjoint is the smooth row-valued map $\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta:U\to(\mathbb C^4)^*$, using the fixed matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], so $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$. In fixed SI units, $\phi$ is in volts, each $A_a$ is in $\mathrm{T\,m}$, $\psi$ is assigned field dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$, and $\chi$ is in webers; these unit labels accompany the maps and do not identify $q$ with a measured charge. For periodic spatial domains, the same component and unit conventions apply to smooth periodic coordinate lifts, with the quotient domain specified by the item using them.

For the SI-normalization bookkeeping, let $c>0$ (m s$^{-1}$), $\hbar>0$ (J s), $\mu_0>0$ (N A$^{-2}$), a real charge parameter $q$ (C), and a mass parameter $m>0$ (kg) be symbolic inputs; put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. In the current SI, $c$ and $h$ are defining constants while $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined; the formula below keeps $\mu_0$ symbolic and assigns it no numerical value. Use the lower-potential convention
$$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),$$
where $A_a$ has units T m, $\phi$ is in volts, and $\mathbf A$ is in T m. Define
$$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c},\qquad a_a=A_a/S_0,\qquad f_{ab}=\partial_aa_b-\partial_ba_a,$$
$$\mu=mc/\hbar,\qquad g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}=q/\sqrt{\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad D_a=\partial_a-ig a_a.$$
Here $D_a$ acts on $\psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4)$ by $(D_a\psi)(x)=\partial_a\psi(x)-ig a_a(x)\psi(x)$, again a smooth map $U\to\mathbb C^4$. Thus $a_a$ and $\mu$ have units m$^{-1}$, $f_{ab}$ has units m$^{-2}$, and $g$ is dimensionless. For $\psi$ with units m$^{-3/2}$, both $-\tfrac14 f_{ab}f^{ab}$ and $\bar\psi(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$ have units m$^{-4}$; their integral over $d^4x$ is dimensionless and represents the action divided by $\hbar$ in this normalization.

For the real smooth gauge-parameter map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R$ in webers, put $\alpha:=\chi/S_0\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ (dimensionless) and use
$$A'_a=A_a+\partial_a\chi,\qquad a'_a=a_a+\partial_a\alpha,\qquad \psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi.$$
The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, with $t$ measured in seconds and $x^0=ct$, and let $T_L^3=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$ be the flat spatial torus with period $L>0$ metres and periodic coordinates $\mathbf x$. Take jointly smooth periodic maps
$$\mathbf A:I\times T_L^3\to\mathbb R^3,\qquad \phi:I\times T_L^3\to\mathbb R,\qquad \rho:I\times T_L^3\to\mathbb R,\qquad \mathbf J:I\times T_L^3\to\mathbb R^3.$$
Write $\dot{\mathbf A}:=\partial_t\mathbf A$ for the time partial derivative at fixed $\mathbf x$, and $\mathbf B:=\nabla\times\mathbf A$. All spatial differential operators below are the periodic coordinate derivatives, and each displayed spatial integral and Hamiltonian is evaluated at a fixed $t\in I$; the time argument is suppressed in the formulas. In SI units, $\mathbf A$ has unit $\mathrm{T\,m}$, $\phi$ has unit $\mathrm V$, $\rho$ has unit $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, and $\mathbf J$ has unit $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. Thus $\dot{\mathbf A}$ and $\nabla\phi$ both have unit $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{T\,m\,s^{-1}}$, and every term of the formal classical Lagrangian density has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. Let $c>0$ have unit $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, let $\mu_0>0$ be the symbolic magnetic constant with unit $\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$, and put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with unit $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$; no numerical value for these constants is adopted. Define the formal classical density
$$\mathcal L=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}|\dot{\mathbf A}+\nabla\phi|^2-\frac1{2\mu_0}|\nabla\times\mathbf A|^2-\rho\phi+\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf A.$$
The canonical momenta are $\boldsymbol\pi_A=\epsilon_0(\dot{\mathbf A}+\nabla\phi)$, with unit $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$, and $\pi_\phi=0$. Periodic integration by parts gives the fixed-time Hamiltonian
$$H(t)=\int_{T_L^3}\left(\frac{|\boldsymbol\pi_A|^2}{2\epsilon_0}+\frac{|\mathbf B|^2}{2\mu_0}+\phi(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho)-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf A\right)d^3\mathbf x.$$
Variation of the multiplier $\phi$ imposes $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho=0$. In Coulomb gauge $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=0$, this becomes $-\Delta\phi=\rho/\epsilon_0$. At each fixed $t$, a smooth periodic solution can exist only if $\int_{T_L^3}\rho(\mathbf x,t)\,d^3\mathbf x=0$. If $\int_{T_L^3}\rho(\mathbf x,t)\,d^3\mathbf x=0$ for every $t\in I$, there is a unique jointly smooth periodic solution with zero spatial mean, whose Fourier coefficients are
$$\widehat\phi_0(t)=0,\qquad \widehat\phi_k(t)=\frac{\widehat\rho_k(t)}{\epsilon_0|2\pi k/L|^2}\quad(k\ne0),\qquad \widehat\rho_k(t)=L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}\rho(\mathbf x,t)e^{-2\pi i k\cdot\mathbf x/L}\,d^3\mathbf x.$$
For every $t\in I$ it satisfies
$$\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int_{T_L^3}|\nabla\phi|^2\,d^3\mathbf x=\frac12\int_{T_L^3}\rho\phi\,d^3\mathbf x=\frac{L^3}{2\epsilon_0}\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{|\widehat\rho_k(t)|^2}{|2\pi k/L|^2}\ge0.$$
This is a classical conditional solver for smooth periodic neutral data; it makes no claim about quantum density products or nonperiodic boundary conditions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the positive symbolic SI constants and units stated in the theorem; jointly smooth periodic maps on $I\times T_L^3$; the fixed-time convention for $\dot{\mathbf A}$; and the Fourier convention stated in the theorem.

[A1] The convention sets $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with positive symbolic SI constants. [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]

[F1] On the normalized torus, the Fourier characters form a complete orthonormal basis and Parseval holds; the theorem's torus measure is normalized to total mass one. [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1], [A2], the smooth periodic data, and periodic boundary conditions.

1.1 Since the displayed density contains no $\dot\phi$, its canonical momentum is $\pi_\phi=\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot\phi=0$. Differentiating with respect to $\dot{\mathbf A}$ gives $\boldsymbol\pi_A=\epsilon_0(\dot{\mathbf A}+\nabla\phi)$. The Legendre expression $\boldsymbol\pi_A\cdot\dot{\mathbf A}-\mathcal L$ equals
$$\frac{|\boldsymbol\pi_A|^2}{2\epsilon_0}-\boldsymbol\pi_A\cdot\nabla\phi+ \frac{|\nabla\times\mathbf A|^2}{2\mu_0}+\rho\phi-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf A.$$
The periodic boundary has no surface term, and integrating $-\boldsymbol\pi_A\cdot\nabla\phi$ gives $\phi\,\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\pi_A$. This yields the displayed $H$; varying the scalar multiplier gives the Gauss constraint. If $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=0$, then $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\pi_A=\epsilon_0\Delta\phi$, so the constraint is $-\Delta\phi=\rho/\epsilon_0$. [A1, given, algebra]

1.2 Integrating this equation over the periodic box at any fixed $t$ gives $0=L^{-3}\int(-\Delta\phi)\,d^3\mathbf x=L^{-3}\epsilon_0^{-1}\int\rho\,d^3\mathbf x$, since each periodic first derivative has equal boundary values on opposite faces. Differentiating the Fourier coefficient under the integral gives $\partial_t^r\widehat\rho_k(t)=L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}\partial_t^r\rho(\mathbf x,t)e^{-2\pi i k\cdot\mathbf x/L}\,d^3\mathbf x$. 2.1 Under Countable Choice [A2], apply [F1] after rescaling $\mathbf x=L\mathbf y$: the characters $e^{2\pi i k\cdot\mathbf x/L}$ form a complete basis for $L^{-3}d^3\mathbf x$. Step 1.2 permits termwise differentiation in space and time to every order, so the resulting real jointly smooth periodic $\phi$ solves $-\Delta\phi=\rho/\epsilon_0$ at every $t$. Reality follows from $\widehat\rho_{-k}(t)=\overline{\widehat\rho_k(t)}$. [A1, A2, F1, step 1.2, given]

$$\int|\nabla\phi|^2=L^3\sum_{k\ne0}|2\pi k/L|^2|\widehat\phi_k|^2,\qquad \int\rho\phi=L^3\sum_{k\ne0}\overline{\widehat\rho_k}\widehat\phi_k.$$

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

## Statement

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every polynomial in $Q$ has a finite absolute moment, computed by finitely many covariance pairings.

3.1 On the diagonal, $T_k(u,\ldots,u)=\mathbb E[(u^{\mathsf T}Q)^k]$. Put $v=u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$. By [F1], $u^{\mathsf T}Q\sim N(0,v)$, so [F3] gives its characteristic function $e^{-vt^2/2}$. 5.1 For $k\ge1$, two symmetric $k$-linear forms agreeing on every diagonal agree everywhere. Indeed, for their difference $A$, expand $$\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^k}\left(\prod_{j=1}^k\varepsilon_j\right)A\!\left(\sum_i\varepsilon_i u_i,\ldots,\sum_i\varepsilon_i u_i\right).$$ In the multilinear expansion, the sum over signs cancels every term unless each label $1,\ldots,k$ occurs an odd number of times among the $k$ slots. Thus every surviving term uses each label once; symmetry makes all $k!$ such terms equal to $A(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, and the sign sum is $2^k k!A(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$. Since the diagonal of $A=T_k-W_k$ vanishes by step 4.1, this sum is zero and $T_k=W_k$. For $k=0$, the empty product has expectation one and $\operatorname{Pair}(0)$ contains just the empty pairing, whose empty product is one, so the formula also holds.
